paragraphs: Chapter 6. Scaling Edge Applications and Elastic Execution

The workshop’s first analysis node now works reliably. More stations begin submitting observation windows, and several technicians request historical comparisons at the same time. A single request is still handled correctly, but requests increasingly wait. The team has access to two additional computers similar to the first one. Can it simply start more copies of the program and obtain three times the useful capacity?

That question introduces scaling. We initially assume compatible Linux nodes on a controlled local network, with similar resources and one administrative owner. They may be small edge computers rather than rack servers. These assumptions let us understand replication, request distribution, and lifecycle management before adding the location and policy differences of the wider continuum in Chapter 7.

The chapter develops one progression: recognize overload, replicate an independent service, give it a stable entry point, use a controller to maintain its instances, and adjust execution as demand changes. Serverless appears near the end as another way to manage when execution environments exist, not as a substitute for understanding their resource needs.
6.1 When one node is no longer enough
6.1.1 More requests are not the same as a slower algorithm

Suppose a simplified analysis worker finishes one independent window every 0.125 seconds when continuously occupied. Its nominal service capacity is eight windows per second. At a steady arrival rate of four windows per second, it may have ample spare capacity. At twelve windows per second, it cannot indefinitely finish all offered work on time. If nothing is rejected or dropped, the unfinished workload grows.

This example describes an assumed worker, not a benchmark of the companion service. Its purpose is to distinguish three quantities. Arrival rate is how much work is offered. Throughput is how much the system completes per unit time. Response time is how long a particular request waits from submission to result. More simultaneous clients can raise offered load without raising completed throughput; the extra work may simply wait or fail.

An application can improve its local implementation, give a worker more resources, or add workers. Increasing the resources of an existing instance is vertical scaling, or scale-up. Increasing the number of instances is horizontal scaling, or scale-out. Adding actual machines is a further resource-provisioning action: several new instances on one already saturated machine do not necessarily create additional capacity. Kubernetes documents workload and node autoscaling as separate concerns. [96, 97]

Figure 6.1. Vertical scaling changes the resources of an instance. Horizontal scaling adds instances. New physical capacity and new service replicas are separate changes; several replicas can still share one constrained node.

Our team first chooses horizontal scaling because independent requests can be sent to compatible workers and two more nodes are available. Three workers with the assumed capacity have an ideal aggregate rate of 24 requests per second. That is a starting estimate, not a promise: the network, input store, result collector, or shared model dependency may impose another limit.
6.1.2 Decide what can be replicated

The easiest component to replicate is one whose request contains the information needed to produce a result and whose processing does not depend on private session state left by an earlier request. Our window-analysis endpoint has this shape. A request sent to worker A or worker B should produce the same numeric result, apart from diagnostic fields such as worker identity.

A continuously running collector is different. Starting three copies that all read the same sensor and append observations can create three deliveries of the same logical event. A database is different again: three independent database containers do not automatically become one consistent database. Replicate the analysis workers first while keeping the input and result responsibilities explicit.

This distinction is useful beyond workshop monitoring. Independent image-classification requests can often be distributed among workers, while a live video stream may carry decoding or tracking state that must remain associated with a session. A speech transcription service may have similar session context. The question is not “can we start another process?” It is “can another instance correctly handle the work that might be sent to it?”
6.2 Replicas need a stable entry point
6.2.1 From three addresses to one service

After starting three workers, the team has three addresses. Giving every technician a list and asking them to choose is inconvenient. It also exposes instance changes to every client. A service entry point separates the logical service from its current workers. A request distributor forwards work to eligible instances, while service discovery supplies the addresses that are currently usable.

Figure 6.2. Clients use one logical entry point while independent requests are distributed to ready replicas. The replicated analysis tier does not automatically replicate the input store or remove a shared result-writing bottleneck.

A first policy can distribute requests round-robin: A, then B, then C, then A again. For similar independent jobs on similar workers, that makes the idea easy to observe. More sophisticated routing can wait until Chapter 8. At this stage, record the worker identifier in every response and check that more than one worker actually serves the workload.

Balance is not guaranteed merely because a service address exists. Some mechanisms select a backend for a connection rather than for each application request; a long-lived connection can consequently keep sending work to one backend. In the first experiment, use multiple clients or independent connections and inspect response identities rather than assuming that every three requests must visit three different workers. Kubernetes Services provide a stable abstraction over a changing set of backends; the exact traffic behavior depends on the service implementation and configuration. [93]
6.2.2 Readiness matters before counting capacity

A container can be running while its application initializes. A model service might be loading weights; an analysis service might be waiting for configuration. Sending ordinary work immediately can produce failures that look like a scaling problem. Count ready workers, not merely created processes.

Kubernetes distinguishes readiness checks, which determine whether a Pod should receive service traffic, from liveness checks, which can trigger a restart when a container is unhealthy. Startup checks provide a separate allowance for initialization. [94] The first lab only needs simple health and readiness endpoints, but their meaning should be explicit. For the supplied stateless service, readiness means it has initialized and can accept analysis requests; it does not certify the freshness of an external sensor history.

Removing a worker also needs an application policy. Stop sending it new work, allow accepted requests to finish where appropriate, and then terminate it. A long-running job may need a durable job record rather than a short drain interval. We introduce the basic lifecycle here because otherwise “reduce the replica count” hides what happens to the requests that were already accepted.
6.3 Managing replicas with Docker Swarm and Kubernetes
6.3.1 Describe what should run instead of starting every instance manually

Manual replication quickly creates bookkeeping. Which node is running version 1.0? Which instance failed? Are there still three usable workers? The team can replace individual start commands with a description of the desired service: its image, configuration, resource settings, and replica count. A management system observes the current deployment and acts to maintain that description.

Docker Swarm models a service as desired state and creates tasks on swarm nodes to realize it. A replicated service specifies how many tasks should run; when a task fails, the manager can create a replacement task if the deployment’s conditions can be satisfied. [89] This illustrates orchestration without requiring the student to implement a controller.
Assume the lab administrator has prepared a small swarm, its private inter-node network, and access to the chosen image. On its manager, an illustrative service command is:

# IMAGE names the image available to every participating worker. docker service create --name analysis --replicas 3 \ --limit-cpu 1 --limit-memory 512m \ --publish published=8080,target=8080 "$IMAGE" docker service ps analysis

The full lab guide explains the environment prerequisites and clean-up. Swarm’s published-port routing mesh can accept a connection at a participating node and forward it to an active service task. The required management and overlay-network ports must be available only where the cluster design permits them. [90, 91] Do not use a public, unrestricted lab network merely to avoid configuring access correctly.

Changing the service to two replicas is now a change to the desired count rather than a request to remove a particular process by hand. Observing the manager’s response helps distinguish the service description from the instances that currently implement it. A one-manager teaching swarm also has a management failure point; replacing an application worker is not the same experiment as losing that manager.
6.3.2 Read Kubernetes through the same questions

Kubernetes addresses the same broad need with a different set of objects. A node supplies execution resources. A Pod is a deployment unit that contains one or more closely associated containers. In our exercise, each analysis Pod contains one worker container. A Deployment maintains the desired set of application replicas and supports controlled updates. A Service provides access to matching ready backends. The control plane manages these objects while node-side components and a container runtime execute the assigned work. [12, 92, 93]

Figure 6.3. A Deployment describes the replicated workload; the control plane maintains it, and nodes run the resulting Pods. The Service carries application access, not the control plane itself. This simplified diagram omits internal components that are not needed for the first deployment.

The important relationship is between description and execution. Editing a Deployment does not directly deliver an HTTP request to a worker. The workload controller maintains replicas; a scheduler selects nodes for unassigned Pods; the node runtime starts containers. Application requests reach workers through the service path. This separates management traffic from useful application traffic before Chapter 9 maps them onto a commercial platform.

Using Docker to build an image does not mean Kubernetes requires Docker Engine as its node runtime. Kubernetes uses its container runtime interface, commonly with runtimes such as containerd or CRI-O. [103] The reusable artifact is the compatible container image; students do not need to learn runtime internals to understand this distinction.
A small excerpt of our Deployment reads as follows:

apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: analysis spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: {app: analysis} template: metadata: labels: {app: analysis} spec: containers: - name: worker image: REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_IMAGE ports: - containerPort: 8080

The executable manifest in the package adds a namespace, resource settings, health checks, and the separate Service. Generate it with an actual authorized image reference; the placeholder above is not a downloadable image. A command such as kubectl apply submits the description. It does not prove that the nodes can pull the image or have enough resources. Inspect Pod status, events, and a real response after submission.

Three replicas need not imply three different machines. Where placement separation matters, configure it and inspect the node assigned to each Pod. For the introductory lab, a single-node cluster can demonstrate the control loop, but it cannot demonstrate physical scale-out. Record that distinction in the experiment rather than counting virtual replicas as new hardware.
6.3.3 Resource requests, limits, and unavailable capacity

A Kubernetes resource request informs placement and resource accounting; a limit constrains consumption according to the resource’s enforcement mechanism. They are not interchangeable. CPU limits can throttle computation, while a memory overrun can lead to termination. Neither setting is a complete response-time guarantee. [95]

Suppose all three available nodes are already occupied by admitted workloads. Increasing the desired replica count to five does not automatically make five workers ready. Some work can remain pending. Node autoscaling, where supported and configured, deals with provisioning or removing underlying nodes; workload autoscaling changes the number of application replicas. [97]

This is particularly important on a physical edge deployment. A workshop with three small computers does not gain a fourth merely because a controller requests it. Options include reserving spare capacity, adding hardware, deferring lower-priority work, or using another execution location. The last option leads to Chapter 7; selecting among the options is developed in Chapter 8.
Figure 6.4. A requested instance needs suitable capacity; changing the replica count alone does not add physical resources.
6.4 From fixed replicas to elasticity
6.4.1 Follow the load, but allow time for the response

A fixed set of three workers can be wasteful during long quiet periods and insufficient during a large burst. Elasticity means adjusting the deployed capacity as demand changes. It requires a measurement, a decision, an action, and time for that action to take effect.

For an introductory policy, measure a service’s load and adjust its desired replica count between stated minimum and maximum values. Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaling supports this kind of control using resource or configured application metrics. CPU-utilization targets depend on the relevant resource requests and require the appropriate metrics pipeline. HPA does not generally mean “add a worker whenever any request waits.” [96]

We can estimate an initial count without pretending to have solved the full control problem. Let arrival rate be lambda, per-worker capacity be mu, and a chosen operating utilization target be u. Under balanced, independent work, a provisional count is:
n = ceil(lambda / (u × mu))

For lambda = 12 requests/s, mu = 8 requests/s, and u = 0.6, the calculation gives three workers. It includes a chosen amount of spare capacity but does not establish a tail-latency guarantee. If arrivals increase to 24 requests/s, the same calculation asks for five workers. A three-node installation must either provide more execution slots with verified capacity or change what it accepts. Rounding the answer down to the available count does not make the original requirement disappear.

Figure 6.5. Elasticity is delayed: observe load, decide, start an instance, and wait for readiness. A burst can build a queue before new capacity becomes useful. Adding an application replica is separate from obtaining another physical node.
6.4.2 Maintain the application while changing it

Scaling, recovery, and updates share lifecycle mechanisms but serve different purposes. Scaling changes capacity. Recovery replaces failed execution. An update changes the application version. A platform may use replicas and readiness checks in each case, yet the success criteria differ.

For the analysis service, a rolling update can introduce a new version while keeping some old workers available. Compare known requests during the transition and include the version in each response. If the output schema changes incompatibly, keeping both versions running may break callers even when every health check passes. Deployment management cannot infer the intended mathematical equivalence of two implementations.

A practical introduction should therefore observe three changes separately: increase the replica count, stop a worker and watch replacement, and update the image. Kubernetes Deployments provide mechanisms for maintaining replicas and managing rollouts, but the application must still supply meaningful checks. [92, 94] Do not combine all three changes in the first experiment; otherwise it becomes difficult to explain an unexpected result.
6.5 Serverless: let the platform manage execution on demand
6.5.1 Why keep every worker running while it is idle?

The workshop adds a daily report generator. Unlike the continuously used analysis endpoint, this component runs briefly after a batch of observations becomes available. Leaving a dedicated worker resident all day may be unnecessary. The developer would rather submit a function or service definition, specify its trigger and constraints, and let a platform arrange execution when work arrives.

This is the motivation for the serverless execution model considered here. Servers still perform the work, but the application developer delegates more instance-management decisions to a platform. Function-as-a-service is one representative form; request-driven serverless containers are another. An event-driven program can also run in a permanently resident process, so “triggered by events” alone does not make an application serverless.

A request-driven path can be understood in five steps: a request arrives, the platform identifies a suitable execution environment, creates or reuses an instance, invokes the application, and returns the result. Afterward the environment may remain available for reuse or be reclaimed. AWS Lambda documents initialization and invocation as distinct lifecycle stages, which helps explain why the first use of an environment can differ from a later use. [100]
Figure 6.6. Reuse can avoid some preparation; execution, dependencies and application state still need explicit treatment.
6.5.2 Serverless can use an edge cluster

The concept is not restricted to a remote cloud. Knative Serving builds on Kubernetes to support request-driven container services, routing, revisions, and automatic scaling. [98] With suitable configuration, its Knative Pod Autoscaler can scale a revision to zero application replicas when idle. [99]

This does not mean the cluster itself disappears. The platform’s control and networking components, the machines, and other resident services still consume resources. On a small edge installation, that overhead can be important. A serverless layer is justified by the execution management it provides, not by an assumption that it is intrinsically lighter than directly running one small service.

The same application image used earlier can illustrate this distinction. Under a fixed Deployment, the developer chooses a resident replica count. Under a Knative Service, the platform can adjust instances according to requests and configured policies. Students need not install the serverless platform from scratch in the introductory exercise; an instructor-provided environment is enough to inspect the application-level behavior.
6.5.3 Cold starts change the comparison

Consider a purely hypothetical service with a warm response time of 100 ms and a cold response time of 1,100 ms. If 10% of requests are cold and the rest warm, the two-point model has a mean of 200 ms. Its 95th percentile is 1,100 ms. The mean alone hides the experience of requests that trigger initialization.

This does not establish those times for any real platform. It shows what to measure. A model service may have substantial initialization because it loads weights, while a small arithmetic function may initialize quickly. Keeping a minimum warm instance, separating a resident model server from short-lived orchestration code, or batching non-urgent work are possible designs. Their resource and latency consequences need comparison rather than an automatic preference for scale-to-zero.

Serverless execution also does not make private in-memory state durable or enlarge an edge site’s physical resources. If the function must consult local sensor history, it still needs a defined data interface and permission. If it writes results, retries must not accidentally duplicate logical actions. Chapter 7 develops those state and communication questions.
6.6 Measure the expansion before claiming success
6.6.1 An additional replica can expose a different bottleneck

Return to workers that can each process eight requests per second. Suppose every completed request must pass through a shared result writer whose capacity is 20 requests per second. Under a simplified pipeline model, the total capacity cannot exceed the smaller of 8n and 20, where n is the worker count.

These are calculated ceilings from invented capacities, not measured throughput. They explain why the fourth worker might add no useful capacity. A real comparison must also account for waiting, transport, varying service times, and failures. Once the bottleneck moves, continuing to replicate the old bottleneck is not an optimization.

For a speech application, the shared dependency could be one model server behind many lightweight request handlers. For a camera deployment, it could be one storage device or uplink. Counting front-end replicas is therefore not enough to explain where the computation actually occurs.

Figure 6.7. With a hypothetical 8 requests/s per analysis worker and a 20 requests/s shared writer, the calculated ceiling is 8, 16, 20 and 20 requests/s. More replicas alone do not remove the writer bottleneck.
6.6.2 A small reproducible scaling experiment

Use the same request set and response checks for one, two, and three workers. Separate warm-up from the measured interval. Record offered requests, completed requests, failures, worker identities, and response-time percentiles. Report the actual node distribution and resource settings. If only one physical host is available, describe the result as a replica-management experiment rather than a multi-node capacity benchmark.

First keep the replica count fixed and increase offered load. Next keep load comparable and change the count. Finally observe a simple recovery or scaling action. This order distinguishes steady-state capacity from the delay involved in changing that capacity.

A convenient local kubectl port-forward connection is useful for testing one accessible application path, but it selects a Pod and is not a valid way to demonstrate Service-wide load distribution. [104] For the distribution experiment, send traffic through the configured Service from an authorized in-cluster client or a properly configured external entry point. The companion guide supplies an in-cluster client path and explains its prerequisites.

The provided Python harness can demonstrate multiple workers and record requests on one machine. Its optional artificial delay is explicitly labeled and is not a model-inference benchmark. Docker, Kubernetes, and Knative behavior must be tested in their respective environments; a successful local HTTP test does not validate their controllers.
Chapter summary

Scaling requires more than creating copies. The application must support the chosen replication pattern, clients need a usable entry point, and a management system must maintain ready instances within available resources. Elasticity adds observation and delayed adjustment; serverless delegates more decisions about instance lifetime while retaining the underlying resource and state problems.

We now know how a pool of similar nodes can serve more independent work. The next question is different: how should an application use resources that differ in capacity, location, data access, and connectivity?
Exercises

6.1 Capacity. A worker handles eight requests/s in a stated test. Estimate the provisional replica count for 12 requests/s at 60% utilization. Explain why neither the estimate nor an HPA setting proves that 95% of requests finish within 200 ms.

6.2 Replication. Which component is easiest to replicate first: a stateless window analyzer, a collector writing unique events, or an in-memory user session service? Explain the additional contract required for each of the other two.

6.3 Observation. A Deployment requests three replicas, but all run on one node. What has been demonstrated? What further observations and configuration are needed to claim physical scale-out or failure-domain separation?

6.4 Elasticity. A site owns only three fully occupied machines. Its controller requests five more Pods. Explain the difference between increasing the desired workload and obtaining capacity, and give two responses available to the application operator.

6.5 Serverless. Compare a continuously used local language model with a once-daily report generator. What startup, state, and idle-resource measurements would inform the choice between resident and on-demand execution?
Chapter 7. Computation Offloading and Device–Edge–Cloud Collaboration

The workshop can now expand its analysis service across several similar local computers. A new deployment changes the problem. A field technician carries a small device between sites, some sites have an accelerator-equipped gateway, and a cloud service stores approved long-term reports. The mobile device cannot always use the nearby gateway, and the uplink is sometimes slow or unavailable. The resources are no longer interchangeable copies in one room.

Should a request run on the device, at a site gateway, or in the cloud? Should the entire request move, or only an expensive stage? Where should the observations and intermediate results remain? Those questions define collaboration across the continuum. Adding resources is still useful, but distance, compatibility, ownership, and data dependencies now influence how they can be used.

This chapter first follows one offloaded computation. It then extends that exchange into a multi-component application and introduces the data consistency needed to make the collaboration meaningful. The goal is a small working design with explicit responsibilities, not a universal algorithm for choosing the best deployment.
7.1 From similar workers to different execution locations
7.1.1 More capacity does not imply the same role

In Chapter 6, the analyzer replicas offered essentially the same interface and could process the same independent input. We deliberately simplified the environment so that replica count and request distribution were the main concerns. A device, a nearby edge node, and a cloud service introduce additional differences.

The device may have direct access to sensors but little spare memory. A local accelerator may run a computation quickly but serve several users. A cloud service may offer more capacity while requiring an uplink and permission to disclose the input. A peer device may be available only while its owner participates. These are not simply different values of the same “speed” parameter.

Before choosing a location, ask whether the task is allowed and able to run there. Is the necessary software compatible? Can the input be accessed? Is memory sufficient? Is the route reachable? Is the transfer permitted? Only candidates that pass these checks should enter a performance comparison. A fast but unauthorized location is not a slightly worse choice; it is outside the permitted design.

A communication link does not itself create a collaboration contract. The participants need compatible interfaces and an agreed meaning for the data. The remainder of the chapter builds those contracts through increasingly complete examples.
7.2 Follow one computation from device to remote service
7.2.1 Offloading is a request with a result

Suppose the technician’s device has collected a window that must be analyzed. In a local design, it calls an analysis function and receives a result. In an offloaded design, it prepares an input representation, sends a request to another execution site, waits for remote processing, and receives the result. The implementation needs a request identifier, an input schema, a result schema, and an explicit timeout or failure outcome.

Our numerical analysis service makes this boundary easy to inspect. The same sample window can be processed by a local function or submitted to the HTTP endpoint introduced in Chapter 5. Compare the numeric results before comparing speed. If the two paths use different windows, units, or analysis versions, the timing difference cannot be interpreted as a clean placement comparison.

Figure 7.1. Offloading includes input preparation, communication, remote waiting and execution, and result return. A local service address and a remote service address can expose the same interface without having the same cost or failure behavior.

A timeout means that the caller did not receive an acceptable result within its waiting policy. It does not prove that the remote worker never executed the request. Repeating a read-only calculation may waste work but does not necessarily change shared state. Repeating a state-changing operation requires a stronger duplicate-handling policy. HTTP’s concept of idempotence concerns the intended effect of repeated requests; choosing a method name is not enough to implement an application’s event identity or result handling. [8]

For this first comparison, keep the operation read-only and bounded. If the remote path is unavailable, report that outcome or use a documented local fallback. Do not silently change the analysis and still describe the result as identical service.
7.2.2 A response-time budget before a placement decision
For one sequential request, a useful first estimate is:
T_remote = T_prepare + D_up / B_up + L_path + T_queue + T_compute + D_down / B_down

Here D_up and D_down are transmitted input and output sizes, and B_up and B_down are effective transfer rates in matching units. L_path captures fixed communication overhead not already counted in transfer time. It can include a measured round-trip baseline for the exchange. Do not add a full measured network duration again if that duration already includes the payload transfer. Connection setup, retries, and serialization belong in the measured path where they occur.

Consider a hypothetical image task. Local execution takes 350 ms. Its remote input is 2 MB, using decimal units, so the payload is 16 megabits. Assume a 20 Mb/s uplink, a 30 ms fixed communication component, 40 ms of remote waiting, 60 ms of remote computation, and a 10 kB result returned at 20 Mb/s. Ignore additional preparation for this first calculation.

The upload takes 800 ms and the result transfer takes 4 ms. Remote completion is therefore 800 + 30 + 40 + 60 + 4 = 934 ms. A faster remote processor has not made the whole request faster. The input transfer dominates the comparison.

Now consider a different design: 20 ms of local preprocessing produces an approved 0.10 MB representation. Its transfer takes 40 ms. If the remaining assumptions still apply, completion is 20 + 40 + 30 + 40 + 60 + 4 = 194 ms. This is promising only if the smaller representation preserves the information the task requires. Its task quality must be evaluated separately; the timing equation cannot establish that.

Figure 7.2. Calculated response components for the hypothetical task: local execution, raw-input offload, and offload after local preprocessing. The values are teaching assumptions, not device or network measurements.

The calculation suggests a practical order of work. First identify what the application must accomplish. Next measure the local path and the complete remote path. Then investigate whether input preparation or placement should change. Moving a model or computation merely because another machine is faster skips the communication part of the application.

Figure 7.3. Changing representation changes the bytes crossing the link and the information available later. These are uncompressed payload calculations at an assumed 10 Mb/s; no network speed or equivalent task quality is measured.
7.2.3 Time, energy, and data disclosure are separate constraints

A wearable task may be acceptable in latency but unacceptable in daily energy use. A site may have ample bandwidth but prohibit uploading a particular data class. A remote path may save device energy while consuming more total energy across the system. These are different questions and require different measurement boundaries.

For a device-energy estimate, account for local preparation, radio use, and the device’s behavior while waiting. For a system-wide estimate, include the remote computation and relevant infrastructure as well. Similarly, bandwidth should state which link is being measured. Reducing traffic to the cloud may increase traffic on the local wireless network.

This chapter compares a few feasible arrangements rather than forcing all outcomes into a single weighted number. Record the required latency, allowed data transfer, minimum task quality, and relevant resource budget. A candidate that satisfies all required conditions can then be compared on the cost or efficiency the application actually values. Chapter 8 develops that decision process.
7.3 Split responsibilities, not just execution time
7.3.1 A multi-stage application has choices at its boundaries

The new field application collects readings, checks their format, computes local features, requests a heavier analysis when needed, and records a report. These steps can be represented as a small task graph. An edge in the graph means that one step needs information produced by another; it is not a requirement to send every intermediate result to the cloud.

Keeping acquisition on the device is natural when it owns the sensor interface. A nearby node might combine streams from several devices or provide a shared accelerator. A cloud service might combine approved reports across sites. The exact allocation depends on the workload. A live camera detector and a weekly vibration report can use similar infrastructure while placing their expensive work differently.

Figure 7.4. Three possible cuts of the same application: all local, local preparation with nearby analysis, and local processing with cloud aggregation. The task boundary determines both the transmitted data and the work that remains local.

A good interface says what crosses each boundary. Does the next component receive raw samples, extracted features, an object reference, or a completed result? Who interprets missing data? Which analysis version produced the output? A reference to an object does not remove the transfer cost if the receiving node must fetch the object from another location.

The application split is also different from the internal split of a neural network. Sending a whole image task to another service is an application-level decision. Dividing one model’s layers across devices introduces additional model-specific mechanisms, which belong in Chapter 11. We can build a useful continuum application without introducing those mechanisms here.
7.3.2 Sequential requests and background work need different timing

If the user must wait for acquisition, analysis, and report generation in sequence, the user-visible time includes those dependencies. If uploading a history is a background task, it need not delay a local answer that uses already available evidence. Drawing the dependency graph prevents the system from waiting for remote work that is not actually needed for the requested result.

For an illustrative three-stage pipeline taking 20, 60, and 10 ms, a single item needs at least 90 ms of stage execution before communication and waiting. If the stages run on different resources and overlap across independent items, the 60 ms stage limits the ideal steady-state pipeline rate to about 16.7 items per second. Summing the stage times and inverting the sum answers a different question: sequential processing without overlap.

A pipeline does not eliminate queues. If the source offers 25 items per second to that 16.7-item/s stage, buffers eventually fill unless the application slows acquisition, changes the processing plan, or rejects work. Device–edge–cloud collaboration therefore needs an explicit pressure signal or overload policy, not just arrows pointing downstream.
Figure 7.5. Only required dependencies delay this response; asynchronous work still consumes resources and needs its own completion policy.
7.3.3 Horizontal collaboration is not another mandatory tier

Two nearby gateways can share an approved summary without involving a central cloud in every exchange. A mobile device can use a peer while it is present. Such horizontal collaboration complements the vertical arrangement of device, site edge, and cloud.

Consider two agricultural plots. Each gateway knows its own local sensor history. A comparison service can request a bounded summary from both, then combine them. Raw records can remain at their sites when the question can be answered from summaries. But the summaries must describe compatible intervals and units. Averaging two means without their sample counts can give a misleading result when the groups have different sizes.

Cooperation also needs a rule for missing participants. A two-site report can say “one site unavailable” rather than present one site’s observations as a regional conclusion. A vehicle or phone that leaves should not be treated as a failed permanent server that a controller is entitled to reclaim. Participation, permission, and availability are part of the application’s interface to the continuum.
7.4 Where data lives, and what consistency means to the application
7.4.1 More execution locations create more versions of knowledge

The technician’s device has recent observations. The site gateway has a longer history. The cloud may have only the records uploaded before a link failure. All three can answer a historical query, but not necessarily from the same evidence. Before introducing a consistency mechanism, ask what the user expects the answer to mean.

A current-status display may require a sufficiently recent local observation. A monthly report can tolerate delayed uploads if it states its completeness. A configuration command may require an acknowledgment that the device has actually applied the change. These requirements should not all be implemented as “read whichever copy responds first.”

A cache speeds access by retaining a copy; it does not define how current that copy must be. A replicated record can survive another node’s failure, but replicas do not automatically agree about concurrent edits. The application needs rules for ownership, update propagation, and acceptable age before it can choose a suitable mechanism.
7.4.2 Keep observation time separate from arrival time

An observation collected at 10:00 may reach the cloud at 10:12 after a disconnection. Its event time remains 10:00. Replacing that time with the arrival time would change the meaning of the history. Record both when needed: one describes the physical observation, the other its delivery.

Suppose a cloud query asks for readings from 10:00 to 10:05 and receives only records that arrived before 10:06. It can return the data available so far, but should not claim that the interval is complete unless the system has a way to establish completeness. A later query may legitimately include delayed observations. Recording the evidence snapshot or collection revision allows users to understand the difference.

A strict instantaneously synchronized view across disconnected sites cannot be obtained by ignoring the disconnection. For a first application, a practical policy is to keep local work available and label remote views with their freshness and coverage. Applications that require coordinated changes must wait for the relevant agreement or refuse the operation during a partition. The right behavior follows from the requested function, not from a universal preference for either availability or freshness.
7.4.3 Desired configuration and applied configuration are different facts

The cloud changes a sampling interval from ten seconds to five seconds. While the device is offline, the cloud knows what it wants but the device still runs the old setting. A useful interface shows both: proposed revision 8 and applied revision 7. Once the device receives, validates, and applies revision 8, it reports that fact.
Figure 7.6. A proposed revision, its application and the report of application are different events.

This is the application-level idea behind a desired/reported-state pattern. AWS IoT Device Shadows provide separate desired and reported objects, but the devices and applications must still implement the behavior that keeps their state meaningful. [20] Chapter 9 will examine the platform representation after the need has been established here.

For the introductory design, assign configuration writes to one authority and use increasing application revision numbers. Do not use arrival order alone when messages can be delayed. If several independent writers must edit the same field, the system needs a conflict rule or coordination mechanism; “keep the last received message” may silently overwrite a newer decision. This chapter introduces the problem and a simple single-writer solution rather than a full distributed-database protocol.
7.5 Disconnection and recovery are part of collaboration
7.5.1 Preserve useful local work

Imagine the field site loses its cloud connection for ten minutes. The device can still reach its local gateway. We choose the following behavior for the teaching application: acquire observations, perform approved local analysis, and retain results; defer the cross-site report; label the cloud view as stale. A local query must not silently switch to a model or database endpoint that is also unreachable.

Offline operation is a property of a particular function and its dependencies. Local code, model artifacts where needed, stored data, and an accessible interface must be available for that function. A local analysis can continue while remote deployment updates are unavailable. A failed local radio link, a failed host, and a failed cloud uplink are different fault cases and should be tested separately.

A phone application gives a useful contrast. It may continue an on-device computation without cloud connectivity but still be suspended by its operating environment. A local network connection does not grant another device unlimited background execution. The collaboration design should name which participant controls continued execution.
7.5.2 Retain an event until its delivery outcome is known

For a simple upload path, store each event in a local persistent pending set. Attempt to deliver it with a stable event key. At the receiver, store that key with the content and return an acknowledgment after the defined acceptance step. Remove or mark the sender’s pending entry only after receiving that acknowledgment.

Figure 7.7. If the receiver stores an event but its acknowledgment is lost, the sender retries the same event key. The receiver recognizes the duplicate and returns the existing acceptance result. This achieves duplicate-safe ingestion only at the defined receiving boundary.

Suppose event device-7 / boot-b / 42 is accepted but the reply is lost. The sender cannot know whether acceptance occurred, so it retries the same key. A receiver that enforces uniqueness can recognize the repeated content. If the key is reused with different content, it should report a conflict rather than silently overwrite a different event.

Local transactional storage can keep related changes together; SQLite, for example, supports explicit transactions for a local database. [101] That does not create a transaction spanning the device, gateway, and cloud. The companion exercise implements a small persistent journal to make the pending and accepted states inspectable; it is not a general exactly-once messaging platform.

An MQTT acknowledgment also should not be confused with a database commit in a downstream application. The broker-level exchange and the application’s acceptance boundary are different. AWS IoT Core’s supported MQTT delivery levels describe messaging behavior, not the completion of arbitrary consumer-side work. [37] The application must decide which acknowledgment establishes the property it needs.
7.5.3 Recovery must not overwhelm current work

When the link returns, ten minutes of buffered data can compete with current observations and interactive requests. Sending the backlog as fast as possible may make the apparently recovered system unusable. A first policy can rate-limit backlog upload, preserve current local service, and expose the remaining pending count.

Storage is finite as well. If the disconnection outlasts the buffer budget, the application must apply a declared retention policy: stop accepting a class of work, discard designated old data, or reduce collection where that is allowed. It should not silently lose arbitrary records and later claim a complete history. This is a requirement decision before it is a clever recovery algorithm.

Do not infer global ordering from a sorted list of unsynchronized device clocks. A source sequence can order one source’s observations; combining multiple sources may require synchronization assumptions and an uncertainty allowance. For our first report, use explicit source intervals and report missing coverage rather than invent a precise causal ordering across devices.
Figure 7.8. Recovery competes with current work; a bounded policy makes catch-up explicit instead of releasing an uncontrolled burst.
7.6 Build and compare a small continuum application

A practical exercise can use two approved endpoints. The originating node prepares a window and calls its local analyzer or the second node’s service using the same request format. An integration test compares deterministic results, records elapsed time, and exposes an unavailable destination. The remote location can initially be another process on the same computer to debug interfaces, but that is not evidence of a real wide-area latency advantage.

Next separate local analysis from asynchronous report export. Use the supplied persistent journal to queue synthetic results while delivery is disabled. Re-enable delivery and intentionally lose one acknowledgment in the test harness. Inspect the pending set, the receiver’s unique records, and the final counts. Restart the journal process between attempts to check that pending work survives. This demonstrates a bounded recovery mechanism without needing to interfere with a real network.

Finally compare two fixed application splits on the same workload. In one, transmit the complete input for remote analysis. In the other, compute an approved representation locally and transmit that. Measure bytes, time, and task quality separately. For numerical windows, a mean may be sufficient for a mean query but insufficient for a question about the sequence of changes. The correct placement and representation depend on the task.

The exercise should end with an architecture description, not a claim that one location is always preferable. Identify where each computation runs, where each important state resides, and which functions remain available under the selected failure. A diagram that marks both the data path and the management path makes those statements easier to inspect.

The synchronization mechanisms here maintain application state. Chapter 14 asks the additional question of who may authorize shared records when several organizations do not accept one unilateral writer; replication alone is not a blockchain.
Chapter summary

The continuum combines different resources through explicit task and data interfaces. Offloading must account for the complete request path, not only remote computation. Splitting an application introduces data-placement and consistency questions, while disconnection turns recovery into part of the normal design.
A small set of fixed, measured arrangements provides the foundation for optimization. Chapter 8 asks how to choose and adapt among such arrangements when requests, resources, and conditions change.
Exercises

7.1 Budget. Recalculate the raw-input offload example at 100 Mb/s upload bandwidth while keeping the stated return link and other terms unchanged. Which path is faster than the 350 ms local baseline? Identify assumptions that could reverse the result.

7.2 Representation. A local gateway uploads one mean per minute instead of the time series. Give one query this supports and one query it may no longer support. How should the system react to the second query?

7.3 Consistency. The cloud desires configuration revision 8, but an offline device last reported revision 7. What can a user interface truthfully display? What event justifies showing revision 8 as applied?

7.4 Recovery. Draw the case where a receiver commits an event and its acknowledgment is lost. Explain the roles of persistent pending state and stable event identity. Why is a transport acknowledgment alone insufficient to prove arbitrary downstream completion?

7.5 Transfer. Design a two-site agricultural comparison or a mobile inspection application. Specify the computation split, evidence locations, one allowed stale view, and one operation that must wait or be refused during disconnection.

paragraphs: Chapter 8. Scheduling and Optimizing Edge Systems

The workshop’s application now has several feasible execution paths. Short analyses can run on a device or a local worker pool. More demanding work can use a shared accelerator, and approved historical reports can run in the cloud. Yet technicians still experience slow responses when a batch report starts at the same time as interactive work. Sometimes the cloud path is faster; sometimes its network delay makes it worse. Adding a worker helps on one day and changes little on another.

The missing ingredient is no longer a deployment mechanism. It is a decision process: which work to admit, where to send it, how much resource to assign, and when to change the arrangement. This chapter uses small examples and measured comparisons to introduce scheduling and optimization from an application perspective. It does not require implementing an operating-system scheduler or solving a large mathematical program.

We begin with an explicit goal, observe the part of the system that prevents it from being met, and compare a few understandable policies. An optimization is useful only if it improves the requested behavior without quietly changing the task, disclosing prohibited data, or creating an unacceptable failure mode.
8.1 Define the decision before choosing a policy
8.1.1 Five decisions often hidden behind the word “scheduling”

The technician asks for a result, while the operator manages applications and machines. These activities have different decision units. A service can be placed on a node long before an individual request arrives. A load balancer routes a request to an existing replica. A worker then decides which queued request to execute. An autoscaler may change the number of replicas available for future requests.

These are not fixed universal timescales, but separating them prevents an unclear experiment. Kubernetes’ scheduler, for example, primarily assigns unscheduled Pods to nodes; it does not automatically choose the order of the application’s internal analysis requests. [102] A study of round-robin request routing should not be described as replacing the Kubernetes scheduler unless it actually changes Pod placement.

Figure 8.1. Placement, scaling, routing, queue scheduling, and admission act on different objects. Application measurements inform policy; a platform executes permitted changes. A working mechanism does not determine which policy best meets the application’s goals.
8.1.2 Requirements first, preference second

Suppose the teaching application has two classes of work. Interactive requests should produce an acceptable answer within a stated response target; historical reports may wait longer. Raw personal data must remain at the site. The system may use a remote service only for approved inputs. These conditions define the feasible designs before comparing cost.

For an illustrative study, set the interactive target to 300 ms for at least 95% of submitted valid requests and require an acceptable result on a fixed evaluation set. These are invented study requirements, not industrial safety limits. An application with different consequences needs different targets. Report how rejected, failed, and timed-out requests count; excluding all difficult requests would make the apparent success rate misleading.

A useful formulation is to seek a lower-cost arrangement among those that satisfy the required quality, response, and data-handling conditions. This avoids assigning arbitrary weights that allow a privacy violation to be “compensated” by a small speedup. Where no candidate satisfies the requirements, report that outcome. The next step may be to change resources or negotiate the requirement, not to label the least-bad candidate compliant.

Cost also needs a boundary. Comparing an owned edge node with a per-request cloud service requires a common workload and accounting period. Hardware allocation, energy, network use, and remote calls may all matter. For a routing decision on equipment that is already powered on, marginal cost can differ from the total cost used for a deployment purchase. State which decision the accounting is intended to support.
Figure 8.2. Constraints filter candidates before preferences rank them; sometimes the correct result is that no candidate satisfies the request.
8.2 Locate the bottleneck with an application trace
8.2.1 A slow response can contain little useful computation

Before changing replica counts, record a request’s important stages: input preparation, transmission, waiting, computation, result transfer, and presentation. Use a monotonic clock for elapsed durations within one process. When different machines contribute timestamps, do not subtract them as though their wall clocks are perfectly synchronized. A first trace can combine client-measured total time with explicitly measured server durations and report the remaining communication overhead.
Consider this invented trace:

Halving computation saves only 20 ms in this trace. Reducing the waiting time by 100 ms has a much larger effect. The trace does not yet tell us why the queue formed: too few workers, a burst, poor routing, or long batch jobs could all contribute. It does tell us where to investigate first.
Figure 8.3. An illustrative request spends most of its time waiting, not computing. Optimization should target the measured limiting stage while preserving the task and result-quality requirements.

For a language-model tool workflow, measure the complete user request as well as individual model calls. Reducing one model call’s time may not matter if the workflow makes unnecessary serial calls or repeatedly retrieves the same data. Model-specific techniques come in Chapter 11; the application-level need to locate time applies already.
Figure 8.4. Intervals must refer to the same request and a consistent clock; a long response need not mean long computation.
8.2.2 Inspect a distribution and its failures

A mean response time hides variation. Record at least a distribution or selected percentiles, together with completion and failure counts. If five of one hundred valid requests time out, those requests belong in the report even if no final response-time value is available for them. Report successful-response latency and the timeout rate separately rather than silently discarding the timeouts.

The numerator of a useful success rate should reflect the application’s task, not simply an HTTP 200 response. For our numeric analyzer, an accepted result must match the declared calculation on the correct input. For a generated report, a rubric can check supported claims, required qualifications, and whether the requested comparison was completed. A policy that returns a cached answer about the wrong interval is not an optimization of the original task.

The workload generator also matters. A closed-loop client waits for its previous response before sending another request, so a slow system can unintentionally reduce its own offered load. An open-loop trace schedules arrivals independently of response completion. Neither is always preferable; use the one that represents the question and state which was used. In a practical classroom experiment, a few explicit burst and steady-load patterns are more informative than one unexplained benchmark number.
8.2.3 A baseline makes improvements interpretable

Begin with a fixed configuration and a simple policy. For example, keep two workers ready, route requests round-robin, and serve each worker’s queue first-come, first-served. Save the request trace and test it again after changing one policy. Keep the analysis version, input distribution, result checks, and network assumptions consistent.

Not every useful comparison changes only one parameter, but a complex change must explain its components. If a new design both adds an accelerator and compresses inputs, report those changes explicitly. Otherwise the reader cannot tell whether the benefit comes from scheduling, hardware, or a changed representation.
8.3 Arrange execution when jobs compete
8.3.1 Queue order can change which requests meet their targets

Suppose a historical job needs 200 ms and an interactive job needs 40 ms. Both are waiting when a single worker becomes available. The historical job’s deadline is 400 ms from now; the interactive job’s deadline is 100 ms. With the historical job first, completions occur at 200 and 240 ms, so the interactive job is late. With the interactive job first, completions occur at 40 and 240 ms, and both meet their deadlines.

Figure 8.5. Two non-preemptive orders for the same assumed jobs. Executing the short-deadline job first meets both stated deadlines in this example. The example does not prove that one policy is optimal for every arrival pattern or objective.

This motivates a deadline-aware queue without requiring scheduling theory. A first-come, first-served policy is easy to understand and does not favor a job that arrives later merely because it is short. An earliest-deadline policy gives urgent work priority. A shortest-estimated-job policy can improve some completion measures but may repeatedly postpone large jobs. Choose the policy according to the application’s commitments and test it under its expected mix.

Our example assumes both jobs are available, durations are known, and execution is non-preemptive. If the batch job is already running and cannot be interrupted, the urgent job may still wait. If duration estimates are wrong, the planned order may fail. These conditions belong beside the example so that a convenient illustration is not mistaken for a universal guarantee.
8.3.2 Admission is part of meeting a promise

A service should not accept an unlimited amount of work and then hope every deadline is met. Before admitting a request, an application can compare its remaining time budget with an estimate of waiting, transfer, and execution. If no allowed path is likely to meet the target, it can return a busy response, offer a deferred result, or invoke a defined lower-cost mode when the user permits it.

Such decisions must preserve the task contract. Replacing a requested detailed analysis with a simple threshold check is acceptable only if it is an explicitly permitted fallback, not if the interface claims the original task was completed. For a classroom design, record fallback use separately from ordinary success.

A bounded queue also protects memory and data freshness. If an arriving status request supersedes an older request for the same display, the application may choose to replace the old queued request. That policy is inappropriate for a historical event log where each event must be retained. The same mechanism can be useful or harmful depending on what the request represents.
8.3.3 Share resources across users, not only requests

Two users may submit very different workloads. One sends frequent tiny queries; another sends fewer large reports. Equal request counts do not necessarily mean equal resource use. A simple multi-user design can maintain per-user limits, separate queues, or a fair rotation, while preserving a bounded amount of service for background work.

The purpose is not to introduce a complicated fairness theory. It is to stop an implementation detail, such as who can open the most connections, from silently becoming the allocation policy. Test a heavy user and a light user together and report each one’s outcomes. An improved aggregate mean can conceal that one user no longer receives useful service.

Resource isolation from Chapter 5 supplies an enforcement boundary, but it does not by itself choose a fair policy. A configured CPU or memory limit also does not establish that an application has enough capacity for its admitted workload. The configuration and admission decision must fit together.
Figure 8.6. The same total work can distribute waiting very differently across users; the policy must state whose requirement it protects.
8.4 Choose placement, routing, and replica count together
8.4.1 Filter candidates before estimating performance

A placement worksheet for one task can list its compatible runtime, memory requirement, data access, permission constraints, and candidate locations. Remove infeasible locations first. Then estimate the full response path using Chapter 7’s budget and current load observations.
Consider three hypothetical candidates for a task with a 250 ms response target:

The cloud has the lowest estimated time but cannot receive this input under the assumed rule. The device and nearby worker have equal estimates for different reasons. A policy can use another relevant criterion, such as device energy or local capacity needed for other work, to choose between them. It should also account for uncertainty: a 210 ms estimate with large variability is not equivalent to an assured 210 ms completion.

If an approved transformed input makes the cloud candidate eligible, reevaluate both its preparation cost and task quality. Do not carry over the old estimate without changing the input assumption. This is how application design and scheduling interact without requiring a single enormous optimization model.
8.4.2 Avoid decisions that ignore the work already sent

A shortest-queue router can be a useful improvement over round-robin, but queue length alone can be misleading when jobs have different durations. An estimate of unfinished work is more informative than a count of requests. A first implementation can track the expected finish time of each worker and add the estimated service time of newly assigned jobs.

If many independent clients all see the same apparently idle worker, they may simultaneously send it new work. The measurement becomes stale immediately. A centralized dispatcher can account for assignments as it makes them; a distributed scheme needs a way to avoid relying only on old observations. This is a useful systems limitation to explain, not a reason to begin the chapter with a complex distributed scheduling algorithm.

For the small teaching simulator, compare two policies on the same arrival trace: round-robin and minimum predicted completion time. The second chooses among eligible workers and updates its prediction after every assignment. Because it uses specified processing times and delays, the results describe the simulator, not measured hardware. A real deployment would need to estimate those quantities and examine estimation error.
8.4.3 Replica count affects both waiting and cost

More replicas can shorten queues if useful work can be distributed and sufficient capacity exists. They also hold memory, may duplicate model weights, and consume resources needed by other services. Fewer replicas can be economical at low load but respond slowly to bursts. The count cannot be chosen separately from worker capacity and startup delay.

A small candidate comparison is often enough for a course project: one, two, or three local replicas, possibly with a permitted remote path. Use the same workload horizon and task quality requirement. Calculate or measure response outcomes and cost for each candidate, then identify which satisfy the stated requirements. There is no need to claim a global optimum over every possible architecture.

The table is an invented decision example, not an experiment. If offline service is also mandatory, the hybrid candidate needs a separate offline test and may not remain feasible. If costs are estimates, report their assumptions and sensitivity. A cheaper plan should not be selected by comparing an hourly cloud charge with an edge device’s purchase price without a common accounting basis.
8.5 Adapt without spending more than the change saves
8.5.1 New capacity takes time to become useful

Suppose a service can currently finish 12 requests/s. A burst offers 18 requests/s while a new worker takes eight seconds to become ready. In a simplified fluid model with no rejection, the backlog increases by (18 - 12) × 8 = 48 requests during startup. If ready capacity then becomes 24 requests/s and arrivals remain at 18, draining that backlog takes another 48 / (24 - 18) = 8 seconds.

Figure 8.7. At 18 arrivals/s and 12 completions/s, an initially empty queue accumulates 48 requests in eight seconds. Raising capacity to 24/s then needs another eight seconds to clear that backlog. This is a calculated fluid model, not a measured queue.

A controller that reacts correctly to load can therefore still miss many short deadlines. Possible responses include retaining headroom, starting capacity earlier when demand is predictable, rejecting or deferring work, or using a permitted ready remote service. Chapter 6 supplied the scaling mechanism; this calculation explains why its timing belongs in the policy.
8.5.2 Moving a component has an amortization period

A service relocation can require transferring artifacts, initializing a model, and moving or reconnecting state. Consider an illustrative 400 MB artifact over a 40 Mb/s link with no cached copy. Transfer alone takes 80 seconds in decimal units. If relocation saves 30 ms on each of the next 1,000 requests, the aggregate service-time saving is only 30 seconds. Under this deliberately simplified non-overlapping cost model, the transfer is not repaid within that workload.

The comparison is not a universal monetary or latency formula. Artifact transfer can overlap other work, the target may already have the image, and saving user-visible tail latency can matter even when aggregate time is small. The point is to identify one-time costs and the horizon over which a benefit occurs. Repeatedly moving an application to follow small load changes can be worse than tolerating a slightly imperfect placement.

Updating or moving a model also may require old and new versions to coexist briefly. Verify the peak resource budget, not only the steady-state budget after the old version disappears. If both versions cannot fit, the update procedure must state how service is interrupted or redirected.

Figure 8.8. The illustrative transfer costs 80 seconds, while each future request saves 0.03 seconds. About 2,667 requests repay the transfer in this non-overlapped accounting model; 1,000 requests save only 30 seconds.
8.5.3 Use simple stability rules before complex policies

A practical first policy can require a meaningful improvement before switching, retain a choice for a minimum interval, and cap how often it changes. This introduces hysteresis: the rule for leaving a state differs from the rule for entering it. The purpose is to avoid changing placement every time two noisy measurements trade places.

For example, switch from the local path only when the remote path is eligible and its estimated saving exceeds a stated threshold for several observations. Switch back when the network becomes unavailable or the local choice becomes clearly preferable. The threshold is a policy parameter to evaluate, not a universal constant.

Device mobility adds a residence-time question. If a moving device will leave a nearby service area before setup is complete, initiating a heavy migration may make little sense. Often a simpler reconnection to a stateless service is enough; other applications need explicit session or state transfer. Choose the level of continuity the application actually requires.
8.6 Compare policies with a reproducible experiment

Begin by writing a testable claim: for example, “under the supplied mixed request trace, separating urgent and batch queues increases the fraction of interactive requests meeting their deadline without preventing batch completion.” This is more informative than “our scheduler improves performance.” State the workload, allowed resources, quality checks, and failure treatment before examining outcomes.

The package contains a deterministic event simulator for queue order and request routing, plus arithmetic checks for the worked examples. Use it to predict behavior, then test selected policies against the real service where the environment is available. Keep simulated service times and measured service times in different files so they cannot be confused in a report.

An initial study can follow three comparisons. First compare first-come, first-served and deadline-based queue order on a known set of jobs. Next compare round-robin and completion-time routing while holding the replica set fixed. Finally add a simple scaling policy and include its startup delay. Changing one level at a time shows which mechanism produced the effect.

Record the result as several outcomes rather than a single unqualified score: completed useful work, response distribution, rejections and failures, per-user behavior, and resource or cost accounting. Repeat a policy under a different load pattern. A policy that works only for the trace used to tune it has not yet demonstrated broad usefulness.

A negative result can be valuable. If a more complicated router gains nothing because every request waits on one shared model endpoint, the next design change may be to address that shared component. Optimization should revise the explanation of the system, not merely search for a setting that produces a favorable chart.
Chapter summary

Scheduling and optimization choose how to use the deployment and collaboration mechanisms already available. The developer should distinguish placement, replica count, request routing, queue order, and admission; observe the relevant bottleneck; and compare policies under explicit requirements.

An application-oriented approach does not need sophisticated algorithms to produce useful insights. Clear baselines, complete time budgets, bounded policies, and honest failure accounting can explain when an improvement is real and when a deployment change is not worth its cost. Chapter 9 examines which of these mechanisms a commercial platform supplies and which decisions remain with the application team.
Exercises

8.1 Decision units. A report says that changing a Kubernetes Deployment from two replicas to four “improved the request scheduler.” Rewrite the claim precisely. What separate measurements would show whether routing or queue scheduling also changed?

8.2 Queue order. Reproduce the 200 ms batch and 40 ms interactive example. Then let the batch start 20 ms before the interactive request arrives and assume it cannot be preempted. What benefit remains available from changing only queue order?

8.3 Feasibility. Use the placement table in Section 8.4. What changes if raw input cannot leave the device, rather than only the site? Why should that condition be checked before choosing the fastest candidate?
8.4 Adaptation. Derive the backlog and drain time in Section 8.5. What happens if capacity after startup reaches only 18 requests/s? What additional action is needed to reduce the existing backlog?

8.5 Evidence. Design a comparison of two routing policies for image analysis or language-model tools. State the baseline, workload, quality checks, cost boundary, and how you will report failures and per-user outcomes.
