paragraphs: Chapter 13. Security, Privacy, and Safety in Edge Systems

A maintenance assistant now works at two workshops. Portable sensors send observations to each site, a local model helps technicians analyze equipment histories, and a vendor distributes software updates. During the demonstration, every device and user was supplied by the development team. In the field, a replacement sensor arrives from another supplier, a contractor needs temporary access, and one site loses its wide-area connection. The application still performs the same calculations, but the assumptions about who can be trusted have changed.

Suppose an incoming record claims to describe a pump in Workshop A. Does that label prove its origin? If a model proposes a useful command, who is allowed to approve it? If an update has a valid signature, is it the right version for this device? These questions concern different properties. Security limits unauthorized access and modification. Privacy concerns what information about people or organizations is collected, inferred, used, and disclosed. Safety concerns unacceptable harm from the system’s behavior, including failures with no attacker at all.

The aim is not to become a cryptographer or to certify an industrial controller. It is to locate enforcement in an application architecture, understand the evidence each mechanism supplies, and test both successful and refused operations. Basic safeguards already appeared in deployment and agent execution. This chapter connects them across devices, local services, and cloud dependencies. The following chapter extends the same reasoning to records shared among organizations.
13.1 Start with the operation and its trust boundaries

Begin with one operation: a technician asks for the history of pump A17. Draw the path from the user interface to the local query service, the observation store, and any remote model. For each crossing, ask who sends information, what the receiver assumes, and what could happen if that assumption is wrong. A trust boundary is not necessarily a network cable. Two containers on the same computer can have different permissions; the same administrator may control computers at several distant sites.

Figure 13.1. Separate device, user, update, and external-service authority. A local network does not give every participant the same rights. The drawing describes a teaching deployment, not a particular product.

A compact threat model connects four items: an asset worth protecting, a capability an adversary might have, an unwanted outcome, and a place that can prevent or detect it. Do not assume every fault is malicious. A duplicate event may result from a lost acknowledgment; an impossible reading may result from a broken sensor. The system needs useful behavior in either case, while investigation distinguishes the causes.

Edge deployments make several assumptions visible. Equipment may be physically accessible outside a locked data center. A phone owner can revoke participation. A gateway may be managed by a vendor while observations belong to a site operator. Connectivity can disappear before new policy reaches the device. These are reasons to describe authorities and dependencies explicitly, not reasons to assume that all remote services are hostile or all local services are safe. NIST’s zero-trust architecture rejects implicit trust based only on physical or network location. [25]

NIST’s IoT capability baseline provides a useful cross-check: device identification, configuration, data protection, interface access, software update, and awareness of cybersecurity state. An application designer should ask which component supplies each needed capability and what happens if it is absent. A gateway can add some protection for a constrained sensor, but cannot retroactively make an unauthenticated measurement originate from a trustworthy device. [23]
13.2 Establish identity, then grant limited authority

An identifier is a name; authentication provides evidence linking a request to an identity. A field such as device_id or site_id is supplied data until the receiver binds it to an authenticated principal. A principal can be a device, user, or service. The binding must come from an enrollment or trust configuration, not from another field in the same untrusted message. In our example, the site registers a sensor’s verification key and records which asset it may describe.

Enrollment answers an earlier question: why should the site accept this key in the first place? A managed installation may check a manufacturer certificate, an administrator-approved inventory, and proof that the device holds the corresponding private key. The operator then grants site-specific permissions. A manufacturer’s statement about device identity does not automatically authorize access to a customer’s records. The course laboratory begins after this enrollment: its in-memory trust configuration is a supplied assumption, not a complete onboarding protocol.

Authorization is the next decision. A technician may read observations from Workshop A but not Workshop B; a sensor may publish its own observations but not install software; an update service may publish artifacts but not retrieve private histories. Write permissions as subject, operation, object, and conditions. This makes “read pump A17 during the approved shift” a different permission from “read every asset forever.” Standards such as ACE-OAuth describe authentication and authorization roles for constrained environments; the exact protocol is less important here than keeping identity evidence separate from the resource decision. [191]
Figure 13.2. Authenticate the principal, bind the request to a resource, and apply the permitted operation and conditions. A claimed device name is not itself authentication.

A local policy enforcement point should remain on the actual access path. A browser interface that hides a button is not enough if the underlying service accepts the same request from another client. Similarly, filtering a language model’s final answer is too late if unauthorized records have already been retrieved into its prompt. Limit the data service’s query before evidence leaves that service. Return errors without exposing whether a protected record exists when even its existence is sensitive.
13.2.1 Revocation and disconnected operation

Identity and permission have a lifecycle: provision, use, rotate, revoke, and retire. Do not copy one administrator secret to every sensor merely to simplify setup. A per-device credential allows a compromised device to be excluded without changing every other device at once, although the system still needs a way to distribute and apply that decision. Protect private keys and policy storage; a policy cannot defend itself if the attacker may replace the trusted key list.

Disconnection exposes a real design trade-off. Suppose a local service receives an access grant at 09:00, valid until 09:15. A central administrator revokes it at 09:01, just after the link fails. If the local service permits cached grants until expiry, the old permission can remain usable for almost fourteen more minutes under the stated clock assumption. It cannot discover the remote revocation from the cached signature. Requiring a live check for every request would instead sacrifice that offline access.

Figure 13.3. A signed cached grant can still be valid under the local policy after a remote revocation that the node has not learned. Expiry bounds a chosen exposure window; it does not provide instant synchronization. Times are teaching assumptions.

Define offline behavior per operation. Reading an already authorized local history may be allowed for a short interval; enrolling a new administrator may require a current online decision. Essential local protective behavior should have its own engineered operating policy, rather than disappearing merely because a remote login service is unavailable. There is no single “allow everything offline” or “stop everything offline” rule that fits all consequences. Clock uncertainty, reboot behavior, and renewal dependencies belong in the design.
13.3 Protect messages without confusing protection with truth

Communication protection must name its endpoints. TLS can protect a connection against eavesdropping and modification and authenticate endpoints according to its configuration. It does not decide which database rows a caller may read. A client also has to validate the expected server identity; disabling certificate verification in a classroom shortcut removes a property the architecture may rely on. Mutual TLS can add client authentication, while application authorization remains a separate check. [178]

Consider an MQTT path from sensor to broker to analytics service. Separate TLS connections protect the two hops, but the broker terminates those connections and can normally access the application payload. If the requirement is that an intermediary must not read or alter protected content, the design needs suitable end-to-end object protection and a key arrangement between the actual producer and consumer. OSCORE is an example of object security for CoAP through intermediaries; it is not a switch that can be applied unchanged to every messaging protocol. [64]

Figure 13.4. Hop protection ends where a connection terminates. Object signatures can preserve source integrity beyond a broker, while confidentiality needs its own design. The two examples show different protected boundaries, not interchangeable protocols.

A digital signature can let the receiver verify a statement using the sender’s public key. The secret signing key must remain protected, and the verifier must obtain the correct public key through a trusted process. A signature does not encrypt the statement. In the lab, the cryptography library performs Ed25519 signing and verification; we do not implement cryptographic arithmetic ourselves. Altering a signed field invalidates verification, but signing a false claim with an authorized key produces a cryptographically valid false claim. [183]
{ "sensor_id": "s1", "site": "A", "boot_id": "b1", "seq": 17, "observed_at": 999, "temperature_mC": 23500 }

This small observation uses integer millidegrees Celsius so the signed laboratory representation contains no floating-point ambiguity. The integer timestamp belongs to a simulated clock, not a real deployment. The full signed envelope also binds its kind, schema version, issuer, issue time, and expiry. Binding the message kind prevents a signed observation from being reinterpreted as an update request. Field names alone do not implement any of these checks; the receiver must verify the envelope and apply source-to-site permissions.
Figure 13.5. The signature authenticates the signed bytes under the chosen key; it does not measure the actual temperature.
13.3.1 Replay, delayed data, and resource pressure

A receiver can see a valid signed message more than once. Use a stable logical event identity, such as issuer, device, boot identifier, and sequence number, and preserve duplicate-handling state across a normal application restart. The same identity and payload is a retry; the same identity with different content is a conflict. The lab stores the event and identity in one local database transaction. This checks a local ingestion invariant, not exactly-once execution of arbitrary remote physical actions.

Freshness is a separate question. A delayed temperature reading may belong in the historical log while being unsuitable for a current-state display. Preserve observation time rather than replacing it with upload time. A compromised sensor can still lie about its time or value; a signed timestamp is an authenticated claim, not an independent clock measurement. Sanity bounds and comparison with other sensors can detect some problems, but do not establish universal physical truth.

Protection consumes resources too. For an invented 100-Hz stream with 24-byte records, adding a 64-byte signature to every record raises application bytes from 2,400 to 8,800 per second before other metadata. Signing batches of ten records reduces that total to 3,040 bytes per second under the same assumptions, but the first record can wait 90 ms for the tenth to arrive. These are payload and collection-delay calculations, not measured cryptographic timing. The choice depends on the deadline and failure behavior of a batch.

Bound message size, parsing depth, queue length, and work admitted per source before expensive processing. Authenticated sources can still overwhelm a shared gateway, accidentally or deliberately. At the same time, a reconnecting device may legitimately upload a backlog. Separate current traffic from historical replay and document which work may be delayed. Resource admission from Chapters 5–8 therefore supports availability as well as performance.
13.4 Keep software trustworthy throughout its lifecycle

A remote update changes executable behavior at a place the developer may never visit. Verify more than the downloaded filename. The receiver needs an authorized publisher, an intact artifact, a compatible target, and an allowed transition from its present version. A manifest binds these facts to a release. The SUIT manifest information model includes target identifiers, digests, sequence information, conditions, and other update metadata; the teaching manifest below uses a deliberately smaller schema. [180]

Suppose the device has accepted security sequence 7 and receives a signed release with sequence 8. The updater verifies the signature against its trusted publisher, checks that the target class matches, hashes the exact artifact bytes, and requires the new sequence to exceed the stored floor. A signed sequence-6 release is still old. A sequence-8 manifest paired with modified bytes is still wrong. The model file, its preprocessing configuration, and any executable loader deserve the same careful provenance treatment as application code.

Figure 13.6. Trust checks decide whether an artifact may be staged; operational checks decide whether it can become the running release. Verification does not establish model quality or safe physical behavior.

A robust deployment separates download, verification, staging, activation, and confirmation. Staging an update before switching helps avoid replacing a working component with a partially downloaded file. Recovery may use a previously approved image, but a security policy must decide which old versions remain acceptable. Operational rollback and protection against rollback attacks are not contradictory: an authorized recovery release can carry a new, explicit policy decision rather than silently accepting any older signed package. Firmware-resilience guidance separates protection, detection, and recovery. [179]

Publisher keys themselves can fail or be compromised. A production update system therefore needs trusted metadata renewal and a recovery path, not just one permanent key compiled into every application. The Update Framework is a useful example of separating signing responsibilities and using signed, versioned, expiring metadata to reduce repository and key-compromise risks. We study the role of these mechanisms, not implement a replacement update framework in a class exercise. [193]
Figure 13.7. Artifact integrity, allowed signer, platform compatibility and runtime health require separate evidence.
13.4.1 Boot, isolation, and remote attestation answer different questions

Secure boot checks permitted software before selected boot stages execute. Measured boot records evidence about what was loaded; recording a measurement and refusing an unapproved image are different actions. Runtime isolation restricts what an application can access while it executes. These mechanisms can complement one another, but none turns an application with a logic error into a correct application. Their roots of trust and the code outside the protected boundary must be identified. [179]

A trusted execution environment can protect selected code and data from specified parts of the surrounding software. Its protection depends on the hardware, configuration, exposed interfaces, and threat model. It is not a promise to prevent every side channel, physical attack, or malicious input. A confidential workload also needs a policy for releasing its key or data to an acceptable execution environment rather than to any machine that claims to have one.
Figure 13.8. Attestation evidence is appraised under a policy; the relying service still makes the access decision.

Remote attestation separates the device producing evidence, the verifier appraising it, and the relying party deciding what to permit. A fresh challenge can help relate a response to the current exchange; a signature alone does not make an old measurement recent. Reference values, endorsement information, and appraisal policy affect the conclusion. The result is evidence for a decision under assumptions, not a universal certificate that the machine or every sensor reading is trustworthy. [181]

For the workshop, an application might release a protected model only after the receiving node presents acceptable evidence. A low-cost sensor might instead rely on a trusted gateway and a much narrower device capability. The textbook does not assume that every edge node has a hardware-backed environment. Ask what must be protected, against whom, and for how long before selecting a mechanism; otherwise expensive assurance can be added to a component that does not control the relevant risk.
13.5 Share edge resources without sharing authority

Chapters 5–6 showed why several services may share one machine. The security view now asks which resources each service may observe or change. A data collector needs its device interface and a write path; a report generator may need only a read-only query interface. A generated analysis program should receive a bounded task snapshot, not the collector’s credentials or the administrator’s container socket. Give each component the access its function requires, rather than making the whole host its implicit workspace.

Containers provide useful isolation mechanisms but share important lower layers. Access to a privileged container-management interface can defeat the intended application boundary; mounting broad host directories can expose data that the service did not otherwise need. Docker’s security documentation explains the daemon’s authority and the importance of configuration. Kubernetes multi-tenancy likewise involves authorization, network and resource policy, and a choice of isolation boundary, not namespaces alone. [174, 182]

Separate confidentiality from interference. Preventing one tenant from reading another tenant’s files does not guarantee that a large inference request cannot delay the other tenant. Memory limits, bounded concurrency, and protected capacity for ingestion help contain resource pressure. They do not by themselves provide hard real-time isolation or eliminate shared hardware failures. A useful classroom comparison asks both “can it read the other data?” and “can its workload disrupt the other service?”

Model inputs and outputs cross these same boundaries. A retrieved manual may contain instructions that are unrelated to the user’s task. The model may also emit an unsafe tool argument without any malicious input. Preserve data as data, validate proposals, and enforce permission in the tool service. For general generated code, a separate restricted worker with no ambient secrets is a design starting point, not a claim of complete containment; in-process text filtering is not a substitute for an isolation boundary. [84, 192]
13.6 Treat privacy as a property of the complete data path

Keeping raw observations local can reduce one disclosure path, but it does not determine everything an application reveals. A wearable summary can expose daily routines; a factory utilization report can reveal production activity; repeated answers can disclose a pattern even when each answer is short. Inventory input records, derived features, embeddings, logs, prompts, model caches, backups, and outputs. Access control should follow the information through these representations, not stop at the raw database.
Figure 13.9. Minimize data at collection, constrain access during processing, and review what leaves through answers, logs, and caches. A shorter representation is not automatically nonsensitive.

A small arithmetic example makes composition visible. Suppose a service returns the exact mean of four approved values as 23 and the exact mean of the same four values plus one withheld value as 24. A caller can recover the fifth value: 5 × 24 − 4 × 23 = 28. Hiding individual rows did not protect that row against these combined queries. The example does not imply that every aggregate is unsafe; it shows why allowed query combinations and side information belong in the policy.

Begin with collection and purpose. Does the application need continuous audio, or only a locally detected event? Does a technician need person-level activity or an equipment-level count? Reducing data can reduce both exposure and communication, but the transformation must preserve information needed for the supported task. A model-generated summary is not a privacy filter simply because the model was instructed to omit secrets. Data-release checks should be independent of the model’s willingness to comply.

Encryption in storage and transit protects bytes against specified unauthorized readers, but an authorized endpoint still processes readable information. Retention policy should cover local files, backups and derived indexes; deleting one row does not prove that every copy or inference has disappeared. Record which deletion operations are implemented and how long replicas can lag. This is an engineering inventory and lifecycle problem, not a claim that a particular policy satisfies every legal requirement.

Differential privacy offers a formal way to limit how much a released result depends on an individual contribution under an explicit definition. It needs a privacy unit, neighboring-data definition, parameters, composition accounting, and utility evaluation; adding arbitrary noise is not enough. Secure aggregation and federated learning solve different parts of a system and do not automatically provide the same guarantee. NIST’s evaluation guidance is a suitable entry point; the core exercise here is identifying the protected unit and release boundary, not deriving a privacy mechanism. [36]
13.7 Authorize a request without confusing it with a safe action

A read-only assistant can give an incorrect explanation. An action-capable assistant can also change the physical environment. The second risk is not removed by improving average model accuracy. A command can be authentic, correctly formatted, and issued by an authorized operator, yet be inappropriate because the device state changed after the operator reviewed it. Operational-technology security therefore has to account for reliability, timing, and safety requirements as well as access control. [24]

Use an abstract simulated actuator to learn the boundary without operating equipment. It has a level from 0 to 100, a state version, a readiness flag, and an observation time. These numbers are artificial interface limits, not safe settings for a pump, fan, vehicle, or building. A proposed change must name the exact target, operation, value, state version, and one-use request identifier. The runtime checks identity and scope, then checks that the required state is recent, matches the expected version, and permits the operation.

Figure 13.10. An action passes separate identity, scope, state and budget checks. Acceptance and the independently observed effect remain different events. The laboratory stops at a simulated permission record.

In the lab, a request based on state version 7 is refused if the supplied current state has version 8 or is more than five simulated seconds old. Reusing the same nonce after acceptance is also refused, including after reopening the local database. The checks illustrate binding approval to a specific request and evidence. They do not prove a physical safety property: the state might be wrong, the controller might be bypassed, or conditions might change between checking and acting on a real device.

A deployed action path needs a protected enforcement point close to the effect, and often an independent interlock or supervisor appropriate to the hazard. Human review helps only if the person sees the exact proposed change and relevant evidence, and has enough information and time to judge it. An approval for one target or version must not be reused for a different one. “Ask a human” is not a complete hazard analysis, just as “ask the model to be careful” is not access control.

Distinguish three records: the desired action, the command acknowledged by the device, and the effect observed afterward. A network acknowledgment does not establish that a motor moved, a valve reached position, or a physical condition became acceptable. Lost feedback may leave the effect uncertain. Retrying an irreversible operation in that state can be worse than reporting uncertainty. The appropriate degraded behavior must follow the application’s consequences; automatically turning every device off is not a universal safe choice.

AI introduces additional uncertainty into this chain. Inputs can shift, training data or retrieved content can be manipulated, and an output can be plausible but unsupported. Keep confidence thresholds, schema checks, provenance checks and operational permission conceptually separate. The adversarial-ML taxonomy offers a map of attacks and mitigations, but a complete edge design also needs ordinary fault handling and domain evaluation. A signature on a model says who released its bytes, not how well it performs on tomorrow’s sensor data. [192]
Figure 13.11. An authorized request can be deferred when current state or operating conditions do not justify the action.
13.8 Use local intelligence for protection, and measure its mistakes

Edge computing can support protection as well as require it. A local gateway can reject malformed records, identify a changed publication rate, or preserve a local warning during a cloud outage. A remote service may correlate patterns across sites that one gateway cannot observe. Combine the views deliberately: local rules can take narrow, reversible actions, while slower cross-site analysis can inform investigation or policy changes. Neither view is complete.

Start with an understandable baseline before adding an AI detector. Count schema failures, source-to-topic mismatches, conflicting duplicates, and queue pressure. Then consider whether a model adds useful information. A backlog upload after disconnection can resemble a malicious burst. Include such legitimate recovery behavior in evaluation rather than training a detector only on quiet normal traffic. Record what the model actually sees: a detector using local traffic cannot justify claims about an attacker’s intent elsewhere.

In this invented evaluation, recall is 90%, the benign false-alarm rate is 1%, and overall accuracy is 98.91%. Yet only 90 of 189 alarms correspond to malicious windows: precision is about 47.62%. A high aggregate accuracy can hide a substantial investigation burden when incidents are uncommon. Changing the population changes that burden even if the conditional detection rates stay the same. These counts are a worked example, not the performance of a trained detector.

Figure 13.12. Local screening and cross-site analysis can cooperate, but observation scope and response authority remain separate. A suspicious pattern may justify review without justifying an irreversible action.

For a protective function, measure time to a useful warning, resources consumed, missed events, false alarms, and the consequences of each response. Detection that starves the data collector undermines the observation it depends on. Automatically blocking a critical device on one anomalous packet may be worse than bounding its rate and asking for review. Use a response policy proportional to the evidence and the application’s consequences, then test it alongside legitimate workload changes.
13.9 Build an enforcement path and test what it cannot prove

The companion exercise uses synthetic workshop records, actual Ed25519 signatures, and local SQLite persistence. No live sensor, network login service, physical actuator, hardware attestation environment, or software installer is operated. The initial trust configuration is supplied. The first experiment receives an approved observation, repeats it, changes signed bytes, and sends an authentic record for an unauthorized site. Students should predict which boundary decides each case before running it.

The second experiment verifies an update manifest against target class, version floor and actual file bytes. It reports eligibility for staging, not a completed installation. The third applies a simulated action gate, then retries the same request after reopening the database and changes the required state. These cases connect cryptographic evidence to application policy. Public keys and signed examples may be inspected; private keys are generated in memory and are not included in the result package.

Keep a deliberate negative control. An authorized test signer changes a plausible temperature to a fabricated 99°C before signing a new event. The value remains within the laboratory’s broad input-sanity range and is accepted. This is the expected limit of source integrity, not a failure of the signature algorithm. The exercise must report “authentic statement accepted; physical truth not checked,” rather than label the value trustworthy. A second negative control in Chapter 14 shows why a valid local history need not be the newest or globally agreed history.

A final design review should produce a small enforcement map, an offline-permission policy, an update and retirement plan, and a list of untested assumptions. Include legitimate retries, recovery bursts, expired permission, lost management connectivity and changed state, not only obviously malformed input. Passing these tests supports the particular implemented checks. It does not establish immunity to all attacks, regulatory compliance, or safe control of a physical process.
13.S Chapter summary

A trustworthy edge application does not obtain all trust from one mechanism. Identity evidence, permission, message integrity, freshness, software provenance, resource isolation, privacy and safe operation answer different questions. Place each check where it can enforce its decision, preserve useful local behavior under a stated policy, and distinguish authentic claims from verified physical effects. Locality changes the available design choices; it does not eliminate responsibility.
13.E Exercises
13.1 Draw the trust boundaries for a phone collecting activity data, a local analysis service, and a remote model. Identify one permission that must be enforced before the model sees data.
13.2 A message contains site_id=A and a valid signature. What additional binding is needed before it can be accepted as an observation for Workshop A?

13.3 A cached grant is valid from 09:00 to 09:15. It is revoked centrally at 09:01 during disconnection. Compare the consequences of permitting cached reads and requiring a live decision. State clock assumptions.
13.4 For the 100-Hz, 24-byte stream in Section 13.3.1, calculate bytes per second with a 64-byte signature per record and per ten-record batch. What new waiting time can batching add?
13.5 An old model artifact has a valid signature and passes an accuracy test. Why may an updater still refuse it? Distinguish security rollback prevention from authorized recovery.
13.6 Explain how secure boot, runtime isolation and remote attestation differ. Give one application property that none of them proves by itself.
13.7 Recover the withheld value when the mean of four values is 23 and the mean after adding a fifth value is 24. What does this show about privacy checks on individual answers?
13.8 An operator approved state version 7, but the actuator reports version 8 before execution. Describe a suitable application response and explain why a valid approval is insufficient.
13.9 Using the detection table in Section 13.8, calculate precision, recall and accuracy. Which number describes how many investigated alarms are genuine in this population?
13.10 Design a legitimate reconnect burst and a suspicious burst that look similar to a rate-only monitor. What additional evidence and response limit would help?
13.11 Run the authentic-false-value negative control. Explain what the signature, scope check and physical measurement validation would each need to establish.
13.12 A report container cannot read another tenant’s directory but can saturate the shared accelerator. Is data isolation enough? Propose an application-oriented test and a bounded mitigation.

paragraphs: Chapter 14. Multi-Party Trust, Blockchains, and Distributed Ledgers

The two workshops now share equipment with a testing laboratory and several manufacturers. Before admitting a replacement device, an operator wants to check its model identifier, certification record, and approved software information. The manufacturer publishes a record, the laboratory publishes a test result, and a later correction changes the status. Different participants keep different copies. Which statement is authoritative, and how can a reader tell whether important history was altered or omitted?

This is a record-governance problem before it is a blockchain problem. If every participant accepts one accountable registry operator, an authenticated database with signed statements and independent audit may be sufficient. If participants require several organizations to maintain a common accepted history under shared rules, a permissioned ledger is a candidate. The number of sensors is not what makes the ledger necessary. The decisive questions concern who may make claims, who may change history, and whose decisions others are willing to rely on.

The chapter develops the mechanisms in that order: verify one statement, inspect a history, agree on accepted updates, place data across the continuum, and evaluate a real IoT registry. Bookkeeping here records certifications, versions, provenance and service receipts; it need not involve money or a token. The laboratory implements signatures and local history checks, not a distributed consensus network. Understanding that boundary is part of understanding what a blockchain adds.
14.1 Specify the disagreement before selecting a ledger

Write a concrete dispute. Manufacturer M says model A passed an approved procedure; Lab L says the uploaded report was superseded; Operator O has cached the earlier status. A useful design must identify who may publish each statement, whether a correction replaces a claim or appends a new one, and how a reader computes the current effective status. “Everyone can see the data” does not answer who is entitled to update it or which conflicts are legitimate.

Separate three objects. A physical device is one installed unit. A device model describes a class of units. A software release is an artifact or set of artifacts that may run on those units. Certification of a model does not directly establish the current software state or physical condition of every deployed unit. This distinction prevents a registry entry from becoming a universal “trustworthy device” label. Bind each decision to the type of object the evidence actually concerns.

Consider the simpler design first. A central registry can authenticate writers, verify their signed statements, enforce update rules, keep backups, and publish checkpoints for independent readers. It is still a central authority for serving and ordering records, and may require external monitoring against omission or inconsistent views. Those may be acceptable responsibilities. Blockchain is not required merely because organizations exchange signatures or keep redundant copies. NIST’s overview is useful precisely because it separates ledger mechanisms from the application assumptions around them. [26]

Figure 14.1. A signature answers who attested to these bytes; a history check answers whether a supplied sequence matches an anchor; agreement determines an accepted sequence under a governance model. None directly measures the physical world.
14.2 Build a verifiable statement

A cryptographic hash maps a byte sequence to a fixed-length digest. For a suitable hash function, finding a different input with the same digest should be infeasible under the relevant cryptographic assumptions. A digest is useful when the expected value comes from a trusted source. If an attacker replaces both the file and the unprotected digest beside it, checking the pair only confirms internal consistency. Hashes do not name an issuer, encrypt a document, or prove the document’s assertions. [26]

A signature adds an authenticated statement under a key. In a registry record, sign the kind of claim, subject, issuer, relevant version or sequence, and the digest of any external report. Readers should not be able to transplant a signature from a test report into a software-deployment instruction. Domain separation and a typed envelope make the intended context explicit. The code uses a fixed application prefix before deterministic encoded bytes, then calls the library’s Ed25519 operation. [183]
Figure 14.2. Bind identity, claim type, subject and content in one signed object. The external report remains separately retrievable and its digest can be checked after retrieval.

Serialization matters because signatures cover bytes, not an abstract drawing of a JSON object. Different whitespace, key order or numeric encodings can change those bytes. A canonicalization scheme defines a shared representation; RFC 8785 provides one such scheme for JSON. The teaching implementation intentionally uses a smaller format: bounded integer values, strings, lists and objects, ASCII field names, deterministic sorting and escaping, and no floating-point values or duplicate keys. It is not advertised as a full RFC 8785 implementation. [184]

Checking a signature also requires a trusted binding between a key and its permitted role. An authorized manufacturer cannot necessarily publish a laboratory’s approval. Key rotation and revocation complicate historical verification: an old signature may remain mathematically verifiable after a credential expires, while new transactions under that credential are no longer accepted. A production archive needs authenticated membership and policy history, reliable acceptance-time evidence, and a way to identify compromised-key periods. Our local history exercise fixes membership and does not implement those lifecycle guarantees.

Return a precise verification result. “Signature valid under registered key K” is narrower than “the device is healthy.” A source can make a false measurement, a test method can be inadequate, or a document can omit relevant facts while still being signed correctly. This is the same distinction as Chapter 13’s authentic false temperature. Provenance helps trace responsibility and investigate claims; it does not replace sensing, independent testing or domain judgment.
Figure 14.3. The signed object binds a stated claim and subject; external content and real-world truth need their own checks.
14.3 From individual records to a protected history

A hash-linked history makes each new entry depend on the preceding entry. For example, record 2 contains the digest of record 1 along with its own content and signature. Changing record 1 breaks the link expected by record 2. Sequence numbers can expose removal or reordering within the supplied history. The reader must still know which starting state and which later checkpoint to trust; a locally consistent prefix can be old, and a dishonest writer may supply different valid branches to different readers.

Figure 14.4. Both branches can contain valid issuer signatures. A previously trusted checkpoint can reject a conflicting or shorter history, but a checkpoint from before the fork cannot choose between later branches.

Work through a two-record example. Record 1 approves a device model; record 2 revokes it. A reader given only record 1 can successfully verify that record’s signature and see an approved status. If the reader already possesses a trusted checkpoint at record 2, the shortened history is detectable. If it has never learned record 2, a signature on record 1 does not reveal the omission. The laboratory executes exactly this contrast. It is a freshness and reference problem, not a weakness in the hash algorithm.

For larger histories, a Merkle tree combines record digests into one root. A reader can verify inclusion of a particular record using a path of sibling hashes rather than downloading every record. An inclusion proof means the record is included under that root; it does not establish that the root is the newest or that an operator showed everyone the same root. Certificate Transparency provides an instructive non-blockchain example of authenticated append-only logs, inclusion and consistency proofs, and monitoring. [190]

Hash linking, signatures, checkpoints and replicated storage are useful building blocks even when a central database remains appropriate. Do not call every one of them a blockchain. Their properties depend on how roots and keys are trusted, how updates become authoritative, and what independent observers can compare. The next question is how multiple participants decide which proposed updates belong in the common history.
Figure 14.5. Integrity, completeness relative to an anchor, and agreement on a branch are different properties.
14.4 Understand ledger roles and the path to acceptance

A distributed ledger maintains shared records across participating nodes under rules for updates and agreement. A blockchain is a family of ledger designs that links blocks of records cryptographically. A replicated database is not automatically a blockchain, and a chain of local hashes is not automatically a distributed ledger. The important application properties are the accepted sequence, validation rules, participant authority, and fault assumptions. Financial transfers are only one possible kind of recorded event. [26]

Keep reading rights separate from writing and validation rights. A ledger may be publicly readable while restricting who can submit particular updates and who can operate validators. Permissionless designs use other admission and resource mechanisms, such as proof-of-work or proof-of-stake, to organize participation. This course focuses on permissioned IoT cooperation: identifiable organizations have explicit roles and governance, and no token is needed merely to teach their shared record problem. Permissioned does not mean every participant is honest or that governance can be omitted.

Figure 14.6. Submission, application validation, agreement on order, and local application of a result are distinct responsibilities. Products may distribute these responsibilities differently. A submitted transaction is not yet a committed application effect.

A useful conceptual path has four stages. A writer constructs and signs a proposed update. Authorized components check the writer and application rules. The ledger protocol establishes the accepted order under its assumptions. Replicas apply accepted changes and readers obtain results. A rejected update may still appear in an audit history as rejected, depending on the system. Never infer business success simply from an HTTP response saying that submission was received.

Hyperledger Fabric is a concrete contrast to a monolithic “every node does everything” picture. Its transaction flow separates proposal execution and endorsement from ordering and validation before commitment. An endorsement is not by itself a committed state change. The ordering service’s documentation also distinguishes crash-fault-tolerant and Byzantine-fault-tolerant options, which have different assumptions about faulty nodes. This architecture is a reference case, not a requirement that an IoT application use Fabric. [185, 187]

Governance supplies rules a protocol cannot invent: who admits validators, how keys and memberships change, which organizations may certify a model, who can correct an erroneous decision, and how software upgrades are authorized. Participants also need a dispute and recovery process. Replicating unclear authority across more nodes does not clarify it. A good design document names the responsible parties as carefully as it names the consensus mechanism.
14.4.1 Why agreement needs fault assumptions

A crash-fault model considers nodes that stop or become unreachable but do not fabricate conflicting protocol messages. A Byzantine-fault model also considers arbitrary misbehavior, including telling two peers different things. An authenticated message can identify the sender of such a contradiction without preventing the contradiction itself. A majority rule designed only for crash faults cannot be promoted to a Byzantine guarantee just by adding signatures. [185]

Use four equally weighted validators as a small teaching example. Under a suitable Byzantine protocol that tolerates at most one faulty validator, a commitment may require three compatible votes. Any two sets of three among four overlap in at least two validators. With at most one faulty member, that overlap contains an honest participant. Protocol rules must ensure that honest participants do not authorize conflicting commitments; voting rounds, locking and membership rules are essential parts of that guarantee. The quorum arithmetic alone is not the protocol.
minimum overlap = max(0, 2q − n); n = 4, q = 3 → overlap ≥ 2

Figure 14.7. With four equally weighted participants, two three-member quorums overlap in at least two. This illustrates a requirement for agreement; it does not implement a consensus protocol or prove liveness.

One unreachable node can leave three available; two unreachable nodes leave only two, so the stated quorum cannot form. During a two-versus-two partition, keeping each side free to commit conflicting decisions would defeat the common-history requirement. A node may still serve an explicitly stale local snapshot, but it should not claim that new updates have been globally committed. Weighted protocols, changing membership and different failure assumptions need their own rules; “three out of four” is not a universal blockchain setting.

In the companion exercise, a static checker verifies three distinct signatures on the same digest. It deliberately does not enforce voting history. If two overlapping signers are instructed to sign conflicting digests, two certificates can pass that checker. This violates the one-fault assumption in the example and demonstrates the missing protocol, not a break of Byzantine consensus. A teaching program should expose this limitation instead of claiming that counting signatures has implemented consensus.
14.5 Place the ledger on the right path of the continuum

A small sensor need not store the full history or validate every transaction. It may produce a signed observation or interact with a gateway that queries a registry on its behalf. More capable nodes can host full replicas or validation services under the organization’s authority. Where a constrained client relies on a gateway’s answer, state that trust explicitly. Receiving a digest from an untrusted relay is not the same as independently verifying the answer against a trusted ledger state.

Keep high-rate telemetry separate from shared trust metadata unless the application has a specific reason to combine them. A certification status may belong on a jointly maintained ledger; raw video and private activity histories usually require different storage and access policies. The application can keep a large report off-chain and record its digest plus an authorized reference on-chain. That commits to selected bytes, not their truth or their future availability. The report still needs storage, access control and retention management.
Figure 14.8. The high-rate data path and the shared trust path have different duties. A digest links the two without transferring ownership, confidentiality, or physical truth into the ledger.

Estimate scale before choosing. Suppose 1,000 sensors each produce a 200-byte record once per second. Raw application payload is 17.28 GB per day in decimal units. Four complete copies already represent 69.12 GB of payload storage per day, before indexes, protocol traffic and historical growth. By contrast, one hypothetical 768-byte status record per device per day is 0.768 MB, 22,500 times smaller. The comparison concerns two different information needs, not a compression technique that preserves every original measurement.

Ledger interaction also adds a different latency boundary. An illustrative update might spend 20 ms in communication to a gateway, 15 ms in checks, 40 ms waiting for batching or scheduling, 30 ms in ordering and commitment, and 20 ms returning confirmation: 125 ms altogether. These invented values are not measurements of DCL, Fabric or any network. Their purpose is to show why an application must distinguish local acknowledgment, transaction submission and confirmed state, and why it should not put a ledger round trip in a fast physical-control loop without a justified design.

Off-chain is not synonymous with private, and on-chain hashes are not automatic anonymization. A low-entropy value can be guessed and hashed until it matches a published digest. Even a well-protected document reference can reveal relationships through public metadata. Fabric’s private-data collections provide one concrete architecture in which selected organizations receive private values while hashes are recorded on a channel ledger; the confidentiality and collection policies remain explicit. This is one design, not a guarantee for every ledger. [186]
Figure 14.9. A digest can verify matching content while exposing low-entropy values to guessing; off-chain storage still needs access control.
14.6 Use shared rules without pretending to automate the physical world

A smart contract expresses rules for proposed changes to shared application state. In the certification example, it might require an authorized laboratory role, a model identifier already registered by a manufacturer, and a report digest before accepting an approval. The code makes the transition checkable and repeatable for participating components. It does not perform the laboratory test or inspect the actual hardware. Fabric distinguishes smart-contract business logic from the surrounding chaincode and transaction machinery. [187]

External information still needs an accountable source. A program that releases a maintenance credit after receiving a signed completion statement knows that an authorized signer submitted the statement; it does not know that a technician repaired the pump correctly. An external data bridge, often called an oracle, moves this trust dependency rather than eliminating it. Keep irreversible effects outside the classroom exercise. For a deployed design, specify how disputed claims, corrected evidence and compensation are handled.

Resource sharing provides another edge-specific example. A phone, gateway, or provider node can offer computation under a task contract specifying input digest, model version, budget and result format. The provider signs an execution receipt; the requester can acknowledge receipt or dispute a result. Such records can support accounting for agreed usage, but they do not independently measure energy or prove inference correctness. A time value reported by the provider remains its claim unless the system supplies stronger measurement evidence.

Participation also needs incentives and exit rules. A user may stop sharing a phone’s battery or revoke access to personal observations. A platform may reward contributed work through credits or reciprocal services without introducing a currency. Neither signatures nor consensus forces a device to remain available or makes a reward scheme fair. The scheduling policies of Chapter 8 must respect these owners and permissions; a technically reachable node is not an unrestricted resource.

An application need not use a ledger for these receipts. If both parties accept one service as the settlement authority, a signed central log may be simpler. A shared ledger is justified only when its joint ordering, audit or governance properties address an actual disagreement requirement. It also brings software maintenance, membership administration and recovery work. Treat these costs as part of the architecture, not as incidental overhead hidden behind the word “decentralized.”
14.7 A real IoT case: the Distributed Compliance Ledger

The Connectivity Standards Alliance’s Distributed Compliance Ledger (DCL) is a useful case because its shared object is device-related trust information rather than a stream of all sensor observations. The Alliance describes a distributed, blockchain-based service for information including product provenance, certification status, and information useful during setup and operation. Reading is public, while writing requires an authorized account. This makes “public” and “permissioned” compatible descriptions. [27]

The official project identifies device-model compliance certification and public-key infrastructure as major use cases. It uses Cosmos SDK application logic and CometBFT-based ledger infrastructure. Its documentation distinguishes validator nodes from nodes that do not participate in consensus, and assigns account roles to authorization policies. These are implementation examples of the roles developed earlier, not details a student must memorize to understand the architecture. Product and repository descriptions here were checked on October 6, 2026. [188]

Figure 14.10. DCL separates authorized publication, replicated validation infrastructure, and public reading. A site uses the returned evidence in its own admission decision; ordinary sensor traffic remains on the application data path. This is a teaching abstraction of the documented roles.

Follow a reader, such as an installation service. It obtains relevant device-model identifiers through an appropriately authenticated setup process, retrieves applicable registry information, and checks the result’s source and freshness under its trust model. It then applies site policy. A simple gateway client may trust an authenticated service endpoint; an independently verifying client needs a supported proof path and a trusted chain state. The project’s reading guide describes access routes, but receiving JSON alone should not be described as independent consensus verification. [189]

The registry does not replace all onboarding evidence. A model-level record does not establish that the physical unit in front of the installer holds the expected device key, runs an approved firmware image, or currently measures accurately. Device authentication, software verification and local admission policy remain separate. Nor does a registry entry grant a technician access to every installed device. This is how the case connects to Chapter 13 rather than overriding its boundaries.

An authorized writer follows a different path: it prepares a transaction of an allowed type, signs with its account key, submits it, and checks the accepted outcome. Publication authority follows account roles and governance; it is not acquired by owning a device that happens to use Matter. The running registry and key-governance procedures are maintained infrastructure. Our synthetic registry records are teaching schemas, not valid DCL transactions, and the laboratory does not publish to or modify a real ledger. [188]

To evaluate this case, map each responsibility back to the book. Chapter 5 supplies execution and isolation choices for participating services. Chapter 6 explains replicas and operation, but replicas alone do not establish shared authoritative history. Chapter 7 explains cached state and synchronization. Chapter 8 contributes capacity and response budgeting. Chapter 9 explains platform responsibility. Chapter 13 supplies identity, authorization and protected software. DCL illustrates their combination around a specific cross-organization record need, rather than a universal replacement for an IoT platform.
14.8 Correct records, revoke authority, and handle offline readers

An append-only history still needs correction. Rather than erasing a false certificate silently, append a new authorized event that identifies the subject, effective change, and relationship to previous evidence. Readers compute the current effective state according to application rules. Historical accountability and present validity are different views of the same records. A correction should not be mistaken for proof that every copy of sensitive old content has been removed.

The meaning of a revocation depends on its object. Revoking a device model’s approval is not identical to revoking a compromised publication key or removing one validator. These operations have different authorities, dissemination paths, and effects on historical records. A current policy might refuse a newly submitted statement from a revoked key while preserving an earlier record accepted before compromise. A complete implementation must authenticate that policy history; examining an issuer-supplied timestamp alone cannot establish when a statement was truly accepted.
Figure 14.11. A reader may hold an authentic approved snapshot while a newer revocation exists elsewhere. Separate signature validity, snapshot age, and knowledge of the latest committed state.

Offline readers face the same trade-off as offline permissions. Suppose a cached approved status has as_of=980 on the teaching clock, the reader checks it at 1000, and policy permits at most 60 seconds of age. It passes the age check. A revocation at 990 that never reached the reader is still unknown. At 1041 the cache is 61 seconds old and must be refused under that policy. The first acceptance does not prove there was no revocation; the later refusal only bounds how long cached evidence may be used.

A signed snapshot from a registry reader is that reader’s authenticated assertion. It is not a light-client proof of ledger commitment unless a verified commitment path is actually provided. Applications can deliberately choose such a trusted-reader design, but must state its authority and failure behavior. A history query may be allowed to return an old, labeled record while enrollment of a new device waits for fresher evidence. Separate these operations instead of describing the whole platform as simply “offline capable.”

Privacy constrains what can be retained in a shared history. Keep unnecessary personal or commercially sensitive information out of permanent shared records in the first place. An off-chain deletion policy still has to address backups, authorized copies and published metadata. A ledger’s tamper evidence and an organization’s data-retention goals may pull in different directions; deciding which information belongs there is an application and governance decision, not a problem solved by hashing everything.
14.9 Compare architectures and test their limits

A final comparison should start from the participants’ requirements rather than select a universally superior technology. A company’s internal maintenance history may have one accepted administrator. A consortium may demand independent endorsements or shared ordering. A public transparency log may let readers audit a central service without distributing every operational decision. Each choice has a different trusted set, recovery process and cost. More replicas can improve some failure outcomes while increasing storage and management effort.
Figure 14.12. Choose the required authority and verification properties first; a replicated ledger is not the default answer to every dispute.

The laboratory begins with a signed model-approval record and appends a signed revocation under fixed issuer membership. It verifies exact bytes, role, sequence and the previous-record digest, and persists accepted records in SQLite. Reopening the database recovers the history. Editing signed content, reordering records, or substituting an unauthorized issuer is refused. The code is a single-process registry with history auditing, not Fabric, DCL or a home-built production blockchain.

Two negative controls are essential. First, audit the one-record approved prefix without a later checkpoint: it passes. Audit that same prefix with the trusted two-record checkpoint: it fails. Second, let the authorized issuer produce two different second records with valid signatures. Both branches pass a local signature-and-link audit from the first record. A later independently trusted checkpoint can select a branch, but the earlier checkpoint cannot. Do not hide these successful local checks; they show precisely why integrity, freshness, and shared agreement are distinct.

Keep the archive’s limitations explicit. It does not prove when a transaction was accepted by an external system, retrieve a live revocation list, rotate validator membership, or keep a consensus network available under partition. Its fixed historical keys permit signature inspection but do not implement a production compromise-time policy. Public keys and signed fixtures are included; private signing keys are ephemeral. A real deployment requires a maintained protocol implementation and governance process rather than an enlarged version of this exercise.

A useful submission combines a design and evidence. State whether one accepted authority is sufficient, what a reader must verify, which data stays off-chain, and what offline behavior is permitted. Include the altered-record, old-prefix and conflicting-branch outcomes, and distinguish the consequences of each. Evaluate record storage, update confirmation and administrative effort separately from the high-rate sensing path. The right conclusion may be that an ordinary database plus signatures meets the requirement with fewer moving parts.
14.S Chapter summary

Multi-party trust begins with the meaning and authority of a statement. Hashes, signatures, authenticated logs, replicated ledgers and consensus supply different evidence. Blockchain becomes relevant when its shared-history and governance properties meet a stated need; it does not make sensors truthful, data private, participation permanent, or physical actions safe. Keeping trust metadata distinct from the application data path allows edge devices, local services and cloud resources to participate according to their capabilities and responsibilities.
14.E Exercises
14.1 Compare an internal maintenance log with a cross-manufacturer certification registry. State which authority assumptions could justify different architectures.
14.2 A device file and the digest stored beside it are both changed. Why can a local digest comparison still pass? What additional trusted reference would help?
14.3 A model-level certificate is valid. List three properties of an individual installed device that still need separate evidence.
14.4 Explain why an inclusion proof under a Merkle root is not a proof that the root is current or universally shown to all readers.
14.5 For four equally weighted validators and a quorum of three, calculate the minimum overlap of two quorums. Which behavioral assumption is still required for the usual one-fault argument?
14.6 A four-validator network splits into two groups of two. Under the stated three-vote rule, distinguish local reading, submitting an update, and confirming a new shared update.

14.7 Calculate daily payload for 1,000 sensors sending 200 bytes each second and compare it with one 768-byte metadata record per sensor per day. Explain why this is not a lossless compression result.
14.8 A smart contract receives a signed “inspection passed” statement. Which facts can it check directly, and which still depend on an external authority or physical test?

14.9 Read the DCL architecture description. Explain how public reading, permissioned writing and validator governance differ. Does a sensor need to be a validator to benefit from registry information?
14.10 A signed approved snapshot is 20 seconds old and policy allows 60 seconds. Can a reader conclude that no newer revocation exists? Describe an offline admission policy and its trade-off.
14.11 Run the old-prefix and conflicting-branch negative controls. Explain exactly which extra property a trusted checkpoint adds, and which global property the local lab still does not implement.
14.12 Design a signed computation receipt for a shared edge worker. Distinguish proof of a provider’s statement, receipt of a result, actual resource use and correctness of the computation.

paragraphs: Appendix A. Laboratory and Project Guide
A.1 Choose a laboratory by its learning objective

The companion directory separates applications that illustrate different mechanisms. Run commands from the named laboratory directory rather than from the book root. Each laboratory has its own README, dependencies, input data, and result provenance. They are not one production system, and completing one does not validate every capability described in the book.

Use institution-approved environments and synthetic or explicitly permitted data. An educational HTTP endpoint is not an authenticated service for public deployment. Do not expose model or development services to an untrusted network merely to make a demonstration easier.
A.2 Observation and deployment foundations

The original roomedge.py foundation accepts records, identifies duplicates, stores local history, constructs bounded evidence, and presents deterministic facts or a replaceable summary. Its stub mode is not a language model. It assumes a trusted local caller and does not implement user authentication, model-directed planning, arbitrary code execution, or a complete agent. Chapter 2’s prepared task walkthrough is a separate synthetic fixture, not a transcript of real model planning.

From Labs/foundation/, start with the local demo and tests documented in its README. From Labs/foundation/systems/, run the small service and client, compare worker/version identifiers, and inspect the persisted event journal. Keep a record of request inputs and returned values before comparing time. The deployment generators create inspectable container, cluster, and Greengrass descriptions; generating a description does not prove that a target cluster or cloud device accepted it.

Commercial-platform work needs an approved account, narrowly scoped credentials, an identified deployment target, compatible artifacts, and a cost boundary. Recheck the dated platform documentation before the laboratory. Do not substitute broad administrator privileges for understanding a permission failure.
A.3 Digital twins: retain observation meaning

The digital-twin replay maps observations to identified entities, retains late history without replacing newer state, detects conflicting duplicate events, and reports stale information. The scenario model is deliberately simple and uses declared assumptions. Store its predicted trajectory separately from observed state. A rendered scene or a predicted value is not evidence of a new physical measurement.

Change arrival order, duplicate one event, and advance the query time while holding observations fixed. Predict the state and freshness result before running the program. Then alter the hypothetical model coefficient and explain why this changes a scenario rather than the recorded history.
A.4 Edge AI: infer first, then compare changes

Begin with the supplied small digit models and saved inputs. The NumPy path reads the laboratory’s documented dense/ReLU parameter arrays; it is not a general interpreter for arbitrary downloaded model files. The optional PyTorch path reproduces training, dynamic-INT8 execution, pruning, and direct-versus-distilled student comparisons using the recorded environment.

The data are cropped 8 × 8 digit images, not a complete camera reader. The three initializations share one sample split; they do not establish variation across writers or field deployments. Keep the weaker distillation result recorded in Chapter 10. A valid experiment need not make an advertised method win. Choose new settings using development/validation data, and name any reused evaluation set rather than describing it as new independent evidence.

Record cold loading separately from warm inference, and model-call time separately from sensor acquisition and application latency. Run a new study into a new directory; never overwrite the supplied measured record while attempting reproduction. Target-board execution, energy, peak memory, static PTQ/QAT, and accelerator performance require separate experiments.
A.5 Collaboration: preserve the comparison boundary

The collaboration experiment reuses Chapter 10 artifacts without retraining. Select the cascade rule on validation inputs and report rescued and damaged predictions as well as total accuracy. The recorded cascade did not improve the local classifier in this setup. The result concerns these models and this inherited sample set, not the general value of collaboration or language models.

Same-model partition tests serialize and reconstruct intermediate values on one CPU host. They establish numerical behavior across that software boundary, not a real network speedup. The optional local language-model adapter can connect to an installed endpoint; interface tests use an explicit HTTP test double. They do not establish actual model quality, memory use, or latency.
A.6 Agents: distinguish proposal, execution and evidence

The Chapter 12 runtime executes local data queries, lexical document retrieval, restricted analysis expressions, result checks, and SQLite task recovery. Its default planner is scripted. The optional model adapter is a separate path that must be evaluated with the selected model and tasks. Neither a script nor an HTTP test double should be labeled model reasoning.

A proposed tool call is not yet an executed action; a stored result identifier does not prove that every sentence citing it is correct. Retain the negative control in which a correct computed 27.25 °C result is accompanied by false 99 °C prose. The narrow format/provenance checks accept the reference, while the independent numeric task check detects the false claim.

Restricted expressions are not a production sandbox for arbitrary Python. A future general-code runner needs a separate isolation design, resource limits, denied-by-default network and file access, and target-environment testing. Task recovery here reopens a local database under one controller; it does not demonstrate exactly-once remote effects or recovery from every physical power-loss scenario.
A.7 Trust: test what each mechanism actually establishes

The trust laboratory performs local signature and hash operations, checks access/update conditions, saves records, and reopens a single-process registry. It also records simulated action approval without operating equipment. Use freshly generated local demonstration keys; keep private keys out of reports and shared packages.

Four negative controls matter: a valid signer can submit a false measurement; an authentic old history can pass a local check without a newer trusted checkpoint; two individually valid signed forks do not constitute consensus; and a fresh cached status can miss a newer remote revocation. Explain these cases before proposing a ledger or an automated actuator.

A static signature-threshold checker is not a distributed consensus implementation. The lab does not deploy DCL, Fabric, smart contracts, hardware attestation, or a live identity infrastructure. Platform examples in Chapter 14 describe documented architectures; consult their versioned sources and validate a real deployment separately.
A.8 A course project beyond the examples

Choose an application with an explicit user, input source, useful output, and reason to consider edge execution. The project may use perception, language, ordinary analytics, or a combination. It need not use a language model or a blockchain merely because these appear in the book.

Establish a baseline before optimizing. State the supported tasks and the quality requirement, then record deployment location, latency, resource use, communication, and at least one failure mode. Compare one meaningful alternative while preserving input and acceptance conditions. A claimed improvement should name its mechanism, its cost, and the condition under which it stops helping.

A proposed assessment allocates 25% to task definition and a working baseline, 25% to the architecture and implementation, 30% to controlled evaluation, and 20% to reproducibility, limitations, and presentation. Treat this as a transparent assessment proposal rather than a claim that every institution uses the same rubric. The final submission should include a short architecture diagram, execution instructions, source/configuration identifiers, allowed data, results, and a known-limitations statement.
